commits.summary: Fail script/lint on warnings, and clear the warnings (#134)
commits.body:
SwiftLint's warnings did not fail `script/lint`, so eighteen of them sat
on main. With `--strict`, a warning fails it as an error does, here and
in CI.

- Five are fixed. The two status bar buttons take their label as a named
closure, a test decodes its bytes with `String(bytes:encoding:)`, and
the search field's `cellClass` is `static` in its final class.
- Thirteen are size and complexity limits, on the choosers, the
JavaScript bridge and the preferences validator. Each is suppressed
where it stands, with `swiftlint:disable:next` or `:this`, and
`file_length` at the top of the two long files, so the limits still
apply to new code. Where a doc comment sits above the declaration, the
suppression goes on the declaration's own line, since a comment between
them detaches the doc comment. Splitting those types is a separate
change.

commits.summary: Make script/lint pass, and run it in CI (#133)
commits.body:
`script/lint` failed on main, and nothing noticed, since CI did not run
it.

- The Swift sources are run through `script/format`. It wraps a few long
lines, puts a blank line before `@testable` imports, and moves a `let`
inside a `case` pattern. No behavior change.
- The one letter variables in `Version` and its tests get names:
`leftToken` and `rightToken`, `leftDigits` and `rightDigits`,
`leftString` and `rightString`, `lowerIndex` and `upperIndex`.
- CI gets a `lint` job beside `build-and-test`, which runs `script/lint`
with SwiftLint from the Brewfile and the Ruby from `.ruby-version`, so a
style or formatting slip fails the pull request that makes it.

commits.summary: Format with std::format and remove text::format (#131)
commits.body:
`text::format` was printf through `vasprintf`. Its 83 calls in 48 files
are now `std::format`, and `text::format` is gone. `text::pad`,
`text::join` and `text::format_size` stay in `text/format.h`. `<format>`
joins the standard headers in the C++ prefix header, where the others
already are, rather than being included in 48 files.

The gain is checking: a literal format string is now checked against its
arguments when the code compiles. printf's `format` attribute only
warned, and only for the arguments it could see.

**The output is meant to be the same, and was checked to be.** Before
any call site changed, a probe formatted values of each call's types
both ways and compared them byte for byte, 64 cases:

- `%.1f` and `%1.f`: rounding, with `%1.f` as `{:1.0f}`
- `%02X`, `%04X`, `%06X`, `%04x`, `%02lX`, `%02zu`: padding, and a
`char` above 127, given `-funsigned-char`
- `%%%02X`: a literal percent
- `%c` of the scope selector's `op_t` and `side_t` enumerations, and
`%d` of the source control status enumeration, each needing a cast,
since `std::format` does not format a plain enumeration as printf
promotes it
- `%.*s`, where the precision argument came first in printf
- `%p` of a typed pointer, which `std::format` takes only as `void
const*`
- Positional `%1$s` as `{0}`
- Literal braces doubled

A second probe compared the five strings with literal braces: the git,
hg and svn test setup scripts with their shell brace expansions, the
`TM_PROPERTIES_PATH` variable, and the relaunch script. It also covered
the two `std::vformat` patterns. A last check confirmed the strings in
the files are exactly the ones the probe tested.

**Where the format came from somewhere else:**

- The bundle item path table, `"Commands/%s.tmCommand"` and the rest,
and the source control drivers' working copy patterns, `"%s/.git"` and
the rest, are now `{}` patterns through `std::vformat`.
- The two pasteboard SQL queries are `constexpr`, so they keep the
compile-time check. One used `%1$s` twice and is now `{0}`.

**One quirk, kept and named:** Find's copy with filename passed
`[item.path UTF8String]`, which is null for an untitled document. printf
wrote `(null)`, while `std::format` would have been handed a null
pointer, which is undefined. The call now writes `(null)` itself, with a
comment. Whether an untitled document should show its display name there
instead is a separate change.

**Smaller things:**

- One call had nothing to format, `text::format("Setting extended
attributes")`, and is now the plain string.
- A `%.*s` over a `std::string` is now the string itself. printf would
have stopped at an embedded null byte, which a command name does not
have.

`OakAssert.mm` builds in the debug configuration only, and
`basic_tree.h`'s dump is a template, so both were also built in debug.
Those test binaries were run there. `layout_test` crashes in debug under
AddressSanitizer, a stack use after scope in `test_basic_tree_delta`,
and does so on `main` too, so it is not from this change. The git, hg
and svn tests, whose setup scripts these are, ran: all three tools are
installed here.

commits.summary: Walk graphemes with a range for over grapheme values (#130)
commits.body:
`diacritics::make_range` hands out a grapheme's base code point on
dereference, and its bytes and length only through the iterator itself,
an overloaded `operator&` and `length()`. So eleven of the loops over it
kept the iterator. This adds `diacritics::graphemes`, a range of values,
and moves ten of those loops onto it, with no change in what counts as a
grapheme.

Four commits, tests first:

1. **What a grapheme is today, pinned down.**
`text/tests/t_diacritics.cc` records the code point, byte offset and
byte length of every step `make_range` takes. The values came from a
probe of the current code, not from expectation:
- Combining marks join their base: `e` and a combining accent is one
step of three bytes.
   - A wide character is one step, and so are a tab and a newline.
- What Core Foundation would join comes apart: `\r\n` in two steps, a
family emoji in seven, the Scotland flag in seven, a thumbs up and its
skin tone in two. The caret's `text::grapheme_end` keeps each of those
whole, so the two notions differ. That is left as it is, and named here
for a decision of its own.
2. **`diacritics::graphemes`.** Each element is a `grapheme_t` holding
`code_point`, `first` and `last`, with `length()`. It sits beside
`make_range`, which stays for the callers that step backwards or jump
ahead. A test checks the two agree on every sample above, and one checks
a value's bytes. Making each value's end one byte past its start fails
both.
3. **Two tests over callers with wide and decomposed characters,** since
the tests over the converted loops used plain ASCII, where every
grapheme is a byte and a wrong offset or length cannot show. `transpose`
keeps a combining accent on its letter and a wide character's bytes in
order. Up and down count a wide character as two columns and an accented
letter as one, landing on the right byte. Both pass on `main`, and each
fails when the code under it is broken on purpose: copying one byte a
grapheme for transpose, and returning the column for the byte offset.
4. **The ten loops,** in the plist writer, find, the key equivalent
formatter, the paragraph layout twice, the layout and selection column
helpers, transpose and the editor's metrics. `*ch` became
`grapheme.code_point`, `&ch` `grapheme.first`, `ch.length()`
`grapheme.length()`.

The eleventh stays: soft wrapping in `text/src/parse.cc` rewinds its
iterator when it backtracks, which a range for cannot do.

A value also has no reference into the iterator to go stale. That is the
shape the spike on Swift Testing over this code found Swift's
interoperability reading wrong.

commits.summary: Find and erase with standard algorithms in the snippet, the event watcher and the bundle index (#129)
commits.body:
Of the eight hand written iterator loops over a whole container, outside
the grapheme loops, three were a find and an erase written out by hand.
They now use the algorithm that says so:

- **The snippet**, `regexp/src/snippet.cc`: replacing a field collected
the iterators of every mirror inside it, then erased them in a second
loop. One `std::erase_if` over the multimap does both.
- **The event watcher's `unwatch`**, `io/src/events.cc`:
`std::ranges::find_if` for the stream with the path and callback, then
the erase, or the log line when there is none.
- **The bundle index's `remove_item`**, `bundles/src/query.cc`:
`std::ranges::find_if` for the item's uuid, then the same callbacks
around the same erase.

The other five stay, since each needs the iterator itself:

- `layout.cc`, three loops, hand each row's iterator to `update_row`.
- `paragraph.cc` inserts at the iterator and returns it.
- The bundle editor selects a row by its position, and keeps looking
after a match whose inner search comes up empty, which a `find_if` would
not.

**Tests.** Neither the snippet's mirror dropping nor `remove_item` had a
test, so the first commit adds one for each, and both pass on `main`
before the change:

- `test_replacing_a_field_drops_the_mirrors_inside_it` uses `${1:a $2}
${2:b}`, where the mirror sits inside field 1 and its field outside.
That is the case only this code handles. In `${1:a ${2:b} $2}`, a later
step drops the mirror anyway, since its field went too. With the erase
made to do nothing, the test fails.
- `test_remove_item` adds an item of its own to the shared index,
removes it, and checks it is gone, then removes it again to show a
missing item is left alone. With the search made to find nothing, the
test fails.

`unwatch` was already covered by the event tests.

commits.summary: Use std::ranges algorithms that take the container for whole-container searches and counts (#128)
commits.body:
Every `std::find`, `find_if`, `find_if_not`, `count`, `count_if` and
`any_of` that took a `begin()` and `end()` pair over a whole container
now passes the container to its `std::ranges::` counterpart: 26 calls in
19 files, across the plist, io, regexp, scope, text, buffer, editor,
bundles, document, Find, OakAppKit, OakCommand and OakTextView
frameworks, the document window, and the shared callbacks header.

Where the only question was whether the result reached `end()`, the call
now asks it directly:

- `std::find(…) != v.end()` became `std::ranges::contains(v, …)`, in the
text view, the callbacks header and the indexed map's tests.
- `std::find_if(…) != v.end()` became `std::ranges::any_of`, for the
executable search in the bundles framework.
- `std::find_if_not(…, isxdigit) == v.end()` became
`std::ranges::all_of(v, isxdigit)`, in the regexp parser.

Each returns the same iterator or count it did, so the code around each
call is unchanged.

The one search over part of a range stays: `io/src/path.cc` searches a
string backwards for a slash, from `rbegin()` to a point short of the
end.

The callbacks header's two new calls sit inside `ASSERTF`, which release
builds compile away, and inside a template, which is only checked where
it is used, so the buffer's tests were built and run in the debug
configuration as well.

The last 39 `NULL`s in code are now `nullptr`, in 17 files. They were

- **Assertion and stack dump code**, `OakDebug`: the sentinels ending

Each is the same swap. Where the October sweep and this one met an

commits.summary: Drop the Homebrew include step from the CI and Benchmarks workflows (#125)
commits.body:
Both workflows wrote `-I/opt/homebrew/include` into `local.rave` before
running `configure`. That was for boost's headers, which `configure`
used to check for under `/usr/local` unless a `local.rave` already
existed, and on Apple Silicon Homebrew lives under `/opt/homebrew`.

Boost left the build in #115, and nothing else the build compiles comes
from Homebrew's include directory. The step goes from both workflows,
and `configure` writes `local.rave` itself, as it does on any fresh
checkout. This pull request's own run is the proof, since it runs the
edited workflows.

commits.summary: Benchmark follow-ups: the right base, every sample kept, a clean report (#124)
commits.body:
Five small follow-ups to the benchmark harness from #123. Nothing here
changes what a benchmark measures.

**The base is the main the pull request was merged onto.** The job
checks out the pull request merged onto main, so comparing against
`origin/main` already isolates the pull request's change, as long as
GitHub has merged it onto the newest main. When main has moved and the
merge ref has not caught up, `origin/main` holds commits the head lacks.
The merge commit's first parent, `HEAD^1`, is always the exact main the
head sits on.

**Every sample is kept.** The plan is to let a few weeks of pull
requests show the noise floor before a threshold fails anything. A job
summary is a table nobody can aggregate, so each run now writes `--json`
and uploads it as an artifact, and the JSON carries the load average as
each run began, which is what tells a noisy sample from a slow one.

**A broken harness fails the job.** The run step piped into `tee` under
the default shell, which has no pipefail, so a failed base build exited
through `tee` and showed green. Naming the shell turns pipefail on. A
slow benchmark still never fails it.

**The report is the report.** The script promises the report alone on
stdout so it can go into the job summary, but the two `ninja` builds,
the base checkout, its submodules and its configure all wrote to stdout
too. The last run on #123 put 364 build lines into the summary ahead of
the table. Those five now write to stderr with the script's progress,
and the report comes out as the seventeen lines it should be.

One thing still left alone: the step that writes the Homebrew include
into `local.rave`. It was what got the job past configure's boost check
while #123's branch predated the boost removal. Now that this is on main
it does nothing, as the same step in `ci.yml` has done nothing since
then, and the two can go together in a pull request of their own.

commits.summary: Benchmark every pull request against main (#123)
commits.body:
Allan wrote TextMate in C++ with performance in mind, and every port of
a hot path to Swift needs a before and after number, not a feeling. This
gives the project its first one.

Every C++ test runner has had a benchmark mode since Allan: a
`benchmark_*` function in a tests folder runs under `-b` instead of the
tests. Six exist, all in `buffer`, and nothing ran them.

`script/benchmark` builds the runners that have a benchmark, runs each a
number of times and reports the median and the fastest run as a table.
`--compare main` builds main in a git worktree too, with a build
directory of its own, runs both turn and turn about so a busy machine
hits both alike, and reports the change per benchmark, calling one
slower or faster past ten percent.

A Benchmarks workflow runs that against main on every pull request,
apart from CI, and writes the report to the job summary. It never fails
the pull request yet. A false red on a shared runner teaches everyone to
ignore the check. Once a few weeks of pull requests have shown the noise
floor, a threshold can fail it.

Same code on both sides on my laptop under load lands within four
percent.

Next, one commit each: a benchmark per hot path that calls the face the
application calls, so the same benchmark measures before and after a
port. The ranker through `TMRanker` first, then scope selectors, parse,
regexp, plist and settings.

commits.summary: Take the CRC-32 from the system's zlib and drop boost from the build (#115)
commits.body:
The build needed boost from Homebrew for one thing: the CRC-32 that the
document attributes carry to check folded ranges against the file, that
the search results carry to check a document has not changed before a
replacement, and that the file framework's bytes offer. The system's
zlib computes the same CRC-32, the standard one with the same
polynomial, initial value, reflection and final XOR, so the checksums
written by earlier builds still match.

That sameness is pinned rather than assumed. A new test checks the bytes
checksum against the standard check values, `0xCBF43926` for `123456789`
among them, and the test was run against boost first and passed, then
against zlib and passed. The five sites use zlib's size_t entry point,
so a buffer longer than four gigabytes is not cut short.

With that, the Brewfile line, the configure check for the boost header
and the README row are gone, and configure writes a `local.rave` with a
comment on what it is for rather than a Homebrew include path. The file
framework links the SDK's zlib by path, the way the document framework
links its sqlite, so a Homebrew zlib on the linker's path is never
picked up. The application and the test executables link
`/usr/lib/libz.1.dylib`.

The build and all thirty four test suites pass.

variables declared the line before. Six of them, the pipe ends in the

Three stay as they were, each with a comment saying why: a block a few

The build and all thirty four test suites pass.

commits.summary: Fork rather than vfork for the assertion stack dump (#112)
commits.body:
The stack dump that a failed assertion prints in the debug build ran
`atos` in a `vfork` child, and built the child's `PATH` there in a
variable length array, which is a Clang extension in C++. The system
deprecates `vfork`, and those were the two warnings the debug compile
carried and the release compile never showed.

The child forks now, and the system's default search path is asked of
`sysctl` before the fork, into a string the parent owns, so the child
only closes, duplicates, sets a signal and executes. Same command, same
three variables in the environment, same dump.

This file is compiled in the debug configuration alone. The object
compiles there without a warning, and the release build and all thirty
four test suites pass as before.

commits.summary: Drop the debug log facility nothing uses (#111)

is declared anywhere in the tree, so no `D()` block could ever have run,
and nothing names any of the four. The one mention left is a 2020
contribution summary about removing an include of it.

The two files go, and the assertion header no longer includes them. They
were compiled in the debug configuration alone, and the assertion object
still compiles there. The release build and all thirty four test suites
pass.

On the way I thought the shared `oak/debug` directory was a second copy
of these files. It is a symbolic link to the framework's sources, so
there was nothing to dedupe.

commits.summary: Read the steady clock where the shared duration timer was (#109)

The last step of the September teardown. The four macros were written
out as the loops they expanded to, one pull request each, and nothing
has named `foreach`, `iterate`, `citerate` or `riterate` since, checked
across the whole repository. The header goes, with its line in the
shared `oak/oak.h` and the one include of it left in the text framework.

The build and all thirty four test suites pass without it.

commits.summary: Stop the file system events tests racing the main queue callback (#107)
commits.body:
The `io_test` crash on CI, three times over two months on pull requests
that touched nothing in io, is found. The file system events tests raced
themselves.

The watcher delivers on the main queue, the runner runs tests on a
worker thread, and the test's callback object kept its paths in a plain
set with no lock. The callback erased from the set on the main thread
while the test thread read it, added to it, and spun on it being empty.
The spin was a run loop call on a thread with no run loop sources, which
returns at once, so the wait burned a core as well. A corrupted set
hangs the test when a path goes missing, or crashes whichever thread
next walks the tree, and a crash on the main thread is what the runner
reported as a crash in no test running. A loop of thirty runs here hung
within the first few.

The set is behind a mutex now, the test waits on a condition variable
with the same five second report of what it is still waiting for, and
after unwatching it lets the main queue come around before its directory
and callback go, so a callback that was mid flight finishes against a
live test. Thirty runs in a row pass, each in three seconds rather than
five.

A probe on the way settled one question: an FSEvents stream on a
dispatch queue delivers no callbacks that were queued behind a busy
queue once it is invalidated, so a late callback into a freed watcher is
not a hazard, in the tests or in the application, which watches and
unwatches on the main thread alone.

commits.summary: Port the HTML output asset policy to Swift (#106)
commits.body:
The asset policy, which bounds what an output page may read from disk,
is Swift. The rules are the ones the C++ had. A path is allowed under a
root by whole path component, after `.` and `..` are folded without
touching the disk, so a link placed inside a root is honored as the
user's doing and a `..` cannot climb out. The roots are the bundle
locations and the target of every link in their Bundles directories,
resolved the way the application resolves a linked bundle's path for
commands, so the pages those commands produce find their assets by that
path.

The scheme handler's face is down to the bundle locations and the
process kill, which are the two things still declared in C++.

The seven tests moved to Swift Testing as they were, over a temporary
directory with files and links of the test's own, and one was added over
the folding itself. The helpers directory is gone with its last header.

commits.summary: Bring back the link preview and the scroll position in HTML output (#105)
commits.body:
Two things the WebKit migration lost in HTML output windows are back,
and one dead file is gone.

The status bar previews a link's target while the pointer is over it,
decoded, as it did before the migration. The legacy web view reported
the hover through its delegate and the new one's delegate has no hook
for it, so a script in the page reports the link under the pointer on
every mouse over, and nothing when the pointer leaves one, through a
small message handler the browser view installs beside the scheme
handler. It works for every page the view shows, with or without the
TextMate object.

A command that refreshes its output into the same window keeps the page
scrolled where the person had it. The old view read the visible rect off
its document view before replacing the content and scrolled back to it
after. The content lives in another process now, so the view asks the
page where it is scrolled, loads the new content once the answer is in,
and scrolls the new page back there once it has loaded.

The not-found page in the resources had been shown by nothing since the
migration dropped the resource load delegate that served it, and is
deleted.

The preview is tested through the handler apart from WebKit: a link
shows decoded, an empty report clears it, and anything that is not a
string clears it.

commits.summary: Port the chooser search field and its accessibility padding to Swift (#104)
commits.body:
The chooser's search field is Swift, with the cell that tells assistive
clients the text has one space before it and one after. That is a
workaround for a VoiceOver fault from 2014 where a search field's first
and last characters were not read, and it stays, since nothing says the
fault is gone.

Each accessibility call is the modern form of the one it replaces: the
value, the character count, the selected and visible ranges in both
directions, the help text, and the nine parameterized ones for strings,
frames, lines and ranges. Every range a client asks about is taken apart
into what falls in a margin and what falls in the real text, the way the
Objective-C did it, as a small value type with tests over each case.

One edge changed. An empty range at a margin, such as the caret at the
very start, had the margin subtracted from it and wrapped below zero in
the Objective-C. It lands at the nearest end of the real text now. A
range past the end, which the Objective-C raised on, is cut down
instead, since raising inside an accessibility call takes the
application down.

With this the chooser framework's Objective-C is the faces alone. The ui
directory is gone.

commits.summary: Port the chooser base class to Swift (#103)
commits.body:
The chooser base class is Swift, with the row view that draws a
selection while the search field has focus, the file row cell, and the
marked up row text. The four choosers are Swift subclasses of a Swift
class now. What a chooser does is unchanged: a floating panel, the
search field in the title bar, the table under it, the footer with the
status and the count, arrow keys in the field moving the table, return
accepting and escape cancelling, the selection kept on its items as the
list changes, and a pick reaching the target through the action.

Two things got simpler for the subclasses. They override the base's row
method and window close plainly, where before they had to name
Objective-C selectors by hand because the base declared its delegate
conformances in a class extension Swift could not see. And the base
hands a subclass the change of first responder as a method call, which
the bundle item chooser overrides for its key equivalent recorder, in
place of a key value observation to pick apart.

One thing the tests caught before it shipped. The base's views were
lazy, as the Objective-C had them, and torn down in the deinitializer; a
chooser that had never shown its search field made one on the way out,
which crashed on forming a weak reference to a deallocating object.
Every view is made with the chooser now.

The search field with its accessibility shim stays Objective-C for now,
as its own piece, beside the faces. The duplicated selected text helper
the two cell views carried is one Swift function. The C++ marked up text
builder and its header are gone, since nothing used them.

The items and their count, the selection across changes, row removal,
the filter reaching the field and the items, a pick reaching the target,
and the default row are tested on the base alone. The two longest
choosers moved their helper sections into extensions so that the
linter's type length rule passes, with no change in what they do.

commits.summary: Port the Select Bundle Item chooser to Swift (#102)
commits.body:
The Select Bundle Item chooser is Swift, the last of the four choosers,
as a subclass of the Objective-C base. Its three tabs, the five fields
it searches by, the key equivalent recorder that takes the search
field's place, the Select and Edit buttons with the option key swapping
the default, what a pick runs and what it remembers are unchanged. The
application's action that opens it hands the scope over as two strings
in place of the C++ context.

Five things the chooser used are C++, and they stand behind two
Objective-C faces. The bundle items face lists the items that apply in a
scope with a settings item spelled out one setting per row and the
eclipsing worked out, the settings in force for a file, the key bindings
from every dictionary the system reads with the selector names turned
into words, the kind of an item by its uuid, a file's icon, and a key
equivalent drawn as its symbols. The scope context face carries the
scope at the caret across from the text view as its two strings and
back.

The rows are a model class of their own, ranking on a concurrent queue
as before, and the cell is a Swift table cell view with the icon, the
name, the location and the shortcut. The walk of the main menu, a menu
item's key in the bundle notation, and the dedupe between menu keys and
key binding files are Swift.

One row icon came back on the way. The settings rows that come from the
preferences looked their icon up through a class the Preferences port
retired, and got none. They show the Variables pane's symbol now.

The ranking in every field, a settings row's value and strikethrough, a
remembered pick, a menu item's key, what a pick is remembered under, the
scope context, and the table asking for a row through its delegate by
selector are tested apart from the window.

With this every chooser is Swift. What is left in Objective-C++ in the
framework is the base class with its search field and row view, the
marked up text builder they share, and the faces, and the base is next.

commits.summary: Port the Open Quickly chooser to Swift (#101)
commits.body:
The Open Quickly chooser is Swift, the third of the four choosers, as a
subclass of the Objective-C base. What it lists on each of its three
tabs, how a typed glob, filter, line or symbol is read, how a row ranks
with a remembered pick first, what a pick carries to the caller, and the
search that fills the list in batches while it walks the project are
unchanged. The document window imports the framework's Swift header in
place of the chooser's own.

Four things the chooser used are C++, and each stands behind a small
Objective-C face. The document face answers for a document's path, name,
identifier, icon and open state, lists the open documents, ranks by
recent use, and walks a directory by the include and exclude settings
that apply to it, with the settings lookup moved into the face from the
chooser. The three document attribute methods the symbol chooser had on
its own face moved here, so the two choosers share them. The source
control face lists the files with local changes and calls back when the
status changes. The glob face matches a typed glob the way the chooser
always read one, and is marked sendable since the ranking uses it from
every thread at once. The paths face, which was the support folder face,
gained the two path rules the rows use.

The rows rank on a concurrent queue as before, each by its own
iteration, and the item says so with an unchecked conformance. The
search keeps its shape: a background walk gathering documents under a
lock, the main queue waiting for the first document that is not already
open so the first batch is on screen with the window, a token to tell a
stale walk from the current one, and a poll at a widening interval.

The filter parsing, the ranking, the directory match, the glob match and
the pick are tested apart from the window, and the table is asked for a
row through its delegate by selector, which is the test that caught the
favorite chooser's crash.

One thing the tests made me look at twice: with no filter the current
document ranks last, not first, which is what the Objective-C did and
what a person wants, since it is the file they are already in.

commits.summary: Port the Open Recent Project chooser to Swift (#100)
commits.body:
The Open Recent Project chooser is Swift, the second of the four
choosers, as a subclass of the Objective-C base. What it lists, how it
ranks, what a pick remembers and what removing a row does are unchanged.
The application's action that opens it imports the chooser framework's
Swift header in place of the file it deleted.

The chooser lives in the chooser framework now rather than in the
application, beside the other three. That is where it belongs, and it is
also what keeps the build clean: a Swift module with a bridging header
of its own that imports another module built with one gets the other's
bridging header chained in, with a deprecation on every build. Inside
the framework there is one bridging header and no chain.

Two refactors come first as their own commits, with no behavior change.
The project state store moved from the document window framework to the
document framework, where the session state already is, since the
chooser framework could not depend on the window framework that depends
on it. The table's key handling moved out of the Objective-C++ header it
shared with C++ default arguments into a plain header of its own, with C
linkage so that Swift finds the functions by name.

The chooser's Swift reads the store, the scope bar and the table actions
through the framework's bridging header. The application's support
folder is the one C++ thing it needs, and it stands behind a one-method
face. Three headers took Swift names and nullability on the way, so the
calls read as they do in Objective-C.

The two lists and the ranking are tested apart from the window: recent
projects newest first and by name among equals, with a vanished one left
out; the Favorites folder's links by name, with a folder link expanded
to the directories inside it; the order kept with no filter; and a
filter ranking by match with an earlier pick for that filter first.

commits.summary: Port the Jump to Symbol chooser to Swift (#98)
commits.body:
Stacked on #97, which it needs merged first.

The Jump to Symbol chooser is Swift, the first of the four choosers, as
a subclass of the Objective-C base. What it lists, how it ranks, which
symbol it selects for the editor's selection, and the window the
document view talks to are unchanged. The document view imports the
framework's Swift header in place of the chooser's own.

Two things the chooser used are declared with C++ types, so each stands
behind a small Objective-C face. The ranker face scores a candidate
against the filter and reports the matched byte ranges. The document
symbols face lists a document's symbols with their positions, parses the
editor's selection string into where each range begins, and answers
three things about the document, which travels as an untyped object. The
ranker's own scoring tests stay in C++, and the face has tests of its
own over the score, the ranges and a miss.

The base got three things on the way, for any Swift subclass: an include
guard by name, since the Swift header carries the bridging header's
imports by source path and the base header reaches the same compile unit
through the include farm; nullability, so the views come across as what
they are; and its initializer declared designated with the window and
coder initializers unavailable, since Swift could not otherwise call up
to it. The two methods a chooser overrides are in the header now as
well, since Swift can only override what it can see.

The marked up row text builder and the layout helpers the choosers share
are Swift now too, beside the Objective-C++ ones the remaining choosers
still use. They go when the base goes.

The selection logic is tested apart from the window: which symbol is at
or before the selection, a reversed range, several ranges, and a
selection before every symbol.

commits.summary: Keep C++ out of the chooser base class header (#97)
commits.body:
A refactor with no behavior change, the first move of the chooser port.

The chooser base class header carried one C++ function, the builder for
a row's marked up text, which takes the ranges the ranker reports. That
made the header Objective-C++, which Swift cannot read. The function now
has a header of its own under `ui/`, and the four choosers that use it
import that.

Why it matters: Objective-C cannot subclass a Swift class, but Swift can
subclass an Objective-C one. So the four choosers, the symbol, favorite,
file and bundle item choosers, port one at a time as Swift subclasses of
the Objective-C base, and the base ports last. For that the base header
has to be plain Objective-C, which it is now.

commits.summary: Port the JavaScript bridge and its shell command to Swift (#96)
commits.body:
The application half of the TextMate object that output pages call is
Swift now: the message handler that answers each call from the page, the
shell command that TextMate.system() starts, and the buffer that
assembles the command's output into whole characters as it streams in.
The page half, the user script, is unchanged.

The command runs through Foundation's Process rather than the C++ spawn,
with the same shell, environment and three pipes, and its output is read
on a background queue and handed to the main one in turn as before. The
buffer holds back a character split across reads and drops bytes that
are not UTF-8, which is what the C++ helper did.

Opening a file at a line or range is the one thing the bridge still
needs from C++, and it stands behind a small Objective-C face.

The bridge's messages have tests of their own now, over the handler
apart from the WebKit message that only WebKit can make: a malformed
message, an unknown method, busy and progress reaching the status bar, a
command answered with its output and status, and input written from the
page reaching the command. The shell command and buffer tests are
ported, the latter over every chunk size from one to sixteen bytes.

With this the HTML output framework's Objective-C++ is down to the asset
policy and the three faces.

commits.summary: Port find, selection and view source in HTML output to Swift (#95)
commits.body:
Find, selection and view source in output windows are Swift now, as an
extension on the web view that answers to the same menu selectors the
text view does. The page is searched through the web view's own find,
the selection comes back through JavaScript, and view source asks the
page for its markup. None of that changed.

The Find window's server, the find and replace pasteboards, the find
preferences and the document controller are all declared with C++ types
the Swift cannot see. They stand behind a small Objective-C face: a
request object that reads what the Find window asked for and reports
what was found, and a handful of class methods for the rest. The face
has its own tests over a stand-in find server.

One finding on the way: the test runner places each test body inside a
namespace and lifts only the imports out, so an Objective-C class a test
needs has to live in a header the test imports.

Next in HTMLOutput is the JavaScript bridge and its shell command, which
finishes the framework.

commits.summary: Port the HTML output scheme handler to Swift (#94)
commits.body:
The scheme handler that carries a running command's output to its page
is Swift now. It keeps the same shape: a process wide registry of jobs
by URL, output streamed to the page as it arrives, a page's own assets
read from disk within the directories it is allowed, and a stopped
command's process group killed.

What stays C++ is the asset policy that bounds the reads, with its
tests, and the bundle locations and the process kill. Those sit behind a
small Objective-C face the bridging header imports.

The scheme name is a property of the handler now rather than a global,
which is the one line that changed in the command runner. The handler's
three tests moved to Swift Testing.

Next in HTMLOutput are the find additions on the web view, and then the
JavaScript bridge and its shell command.

commits.summary: Move the HTML output window controller to Swift (#93)
commits.body:
The next piece of `HTMLOutput`, and the smallest: the window a command's
output gets when output goes to a window of its own. With it,
`HTMLOutputWindow` is a framework with nothing but Swift in it, the way
`CommitWindow` is.

The controller makes the window, a third of the main screen's width and
three fifths of its height in the middle, fills it with the output view,
binds the title and the edited mark to the view, asks before closing a
window whose command is still running and closes itself once the command
has stopped, and keeps itself alive from showing until a turn of the run
loop after closing, since nothing else holds it once the command has
finished. All as before. The Objective-C name stays,
`HTMLOutputWindowController` with `initWithIdentifier:`, so the command
runner and the document window change nothing. The framework's umbrella
header hands out the Swift header beside `HTMLOutput`'s, since the view
the controller holds is that framework's. Two Objective-C++ imports the
controller never used, the command runner and the string conversions,
are gone from its build file too.

In Ruby terms: a controller whose one model is the view, moved whole,
with the two lines that build the window and the one that decides
whether a close may proceed.

Tests, four, for the first time: the window holds the view and is not
released on close, the title follows the view's, each identifier
remembers its own frame, and a window with no command running closes at
once.

commits.summary: Stop the HTML output view appending a trace log under /tmp (#92)
commits.body:
`SchemeTrace` was debug logging from the WebKit migration that never
came out: a function that appended a line to `/tmp/tm_wk.log` on every
failed navigation, in every build, so every copy of the application grew
a log file in the temporary directory. After the view port in #91
nothing called it any more, and the one line it wrote that was worth
having, which navigation failed and why, had gone with the caller.

The function and its declaration are gone. The line is back as a debug
entry in the unified log, from the browser view's failed navigation
handler, with the URL and the error's domain and code, where it is there
for anyone looking with `log stream` and invisible otherwise. The
framework's tests pass and the application builds.

commits.summary: Move the HTML output view to Swift (#91)
commits.body:
The next piece of the Swift candidates list, and the one that finishes a
framework's view layer: `HTMLOutput`'s browser view around the web view
and its status bar, the output view that knows the command it shows, the
delegate that handles a page's alerts, open panels, new windows and
closing, and the auto scroll helper. Four Objective-C++ files, about 600
lines, become three Swift files, with a bridging header beside them.

## The shape

- The Objective-C names stay: `OakHTMLOutputView`, `HOBrowserView`,
`HOWebViewDelegateHelper`. The command runner, the document window and
the output window call them as before, through the header the Swift
compiler writes, which the framework's umbrella header now hands out.
One signature changed: the command's environment crosses as a dictionary
rather than a `std::map`, since Swift cannot see the map, and the
command runner builds the dictionary in four lines.
- The JavaScript bridge and the scheme handler stay Objective-C++ behind
faces the Swift can see. The bridge gains a dictionary setter for the
environment and keeps its map face for the shell command and the tests.
The two headers carry include guards by name, because the generated
Swift header imports them by source path while callers import the farm's
copies, and `#import` cannot tell the two apart.
- Everything the Objective-C++ did is done the same way: the window
binding on `mainFrameTitle` and `runningCommand` through KVO compliant
properties, the refresher's observation of `visible`, the key event
swallowing and its reasoning, swipe navigation, the load error page, the
print margins, the txmt link handling with the project added, the first
responder search after a redirect to a PDF.
- The `WKUIDelegate` alerts use the async forms, which is what Swift 6
matches cleanly, with the same sheets behind them.

## One behavior change, called out

`closeAsIfRequestedByPage` sent the user interface delegate
`webViewClose:`, a selector no delegate implements, so it would have
raised an unrecognized selector exception whenever the command runner
discarded an output window without a document window to hand it to. It
now sends `webViewDidClose:`, the message WebKit defines and the
delegate implements. Porting the line as it stood would have ported a
crash.

## Tests

The view had none and has eight, over its face: what it says before and
after a load with and without a command identifier, the title falling
back to the command's name until the page has one, the key path the
title follows, stopping with nothing loaded, and progress updates
toggled repeatedly. The framework's fourteen tests pass, and the
application builds and runs.

## Left in Objective-C++

`HOJSBridge` and `HOJSShellCommand`, which spawn processes and buffer
UTF-8 through the C++ helpers, `HOFileHandleSchemeHandler`, which reads
bundle locations and the asset policy, and the find additions on
`WKWebView`, which use the C++ find flags. Each has a narrow face now,
which is the shape the next pull request needs. Also noticed on the way
and left alone: `SchemeTrace` appends to `/tmp/tm_wk.log` in every
build, which is its own pull request.

commits.summary: Run the person's own code on the Ruby their project pins (#90)
commits.body:
Command-R and the Ruby bundle's run commands ran everything on
`TM_RUBY`, the Ruby bundle commands run on, which the application pins
and which has nothing to do with the project in the window. The command
environment now carries `TM_PROJECT_RUBY`, the Ruby rv resolves for the
project from its `.ruby-version` or `.tool-versions`, and the Ruby
bundle prefers it for the person's own code. Bundle commands keep
running on `TM_RUBY`. The pin wins over a `TM_RUBY` the person set by
hand, since the pin is their own statement about that project, and
`TM_RUBY` stays the escape hatch for bundles.

## How

- `Frameworks/io/src/project_ruby`: runs the Runtimes Ruby bundle's
`project_ruby` for a directory and reads its answer, `ruby`, `missing`
with the version and the file that pins it, `none` or `error`, the way
`ruby_runtime` reads the launch resolver's. A cached lookup keeps the
answer per directory until its fingerprint moves: the modification times
of every `.ruby-version` and `.tool-versions` from the directory up to
the root and in the home directory, plus the directories of the Ruby
managers, which is how an install the person makes is noticed without
asking rv again on every command. In Ruby terms, a memoized method whose
cache key is a string of stats.
- The document window controller adds `TM_PROJECT_RUBY` where it adds
`TM_PROJECT_DIRECTORY`, from the project directory when the window has
one and from the document's own directory when it is a lone file, which
is what a script run with Command-R usually is.
- A pin that names a version not installed is not installed on
Command-R, since that would be a surprise. A notice on the banner names
the file that pins, as a link that shows it in Finder, the version, and
the `rv ruby install` that would put it there, keyed per project so it
posts once, and it is taken down on its own once the install has
happened, because the manager directory's time moves the fingerprint and
the next answer is `ruby`.

## The banner

- A notice's text is inline Markdown: a path or a command in backticks
draws monospaced, a name in double asterisks draws medium, and a link
draws as one. Plain text draws as it did, so the runtime notices are
unchanged.
- The text is an AppKit text view inside the SwiftUI banner, since
SwiftUI's own text neither changes the cursor over a link nor says where
it was clicked, and a text field tracks the cursor over a link only
while editing. The text view shows the hand at rest, keeps the text
selectable, and hands a clicked file link to Finder. The banner tells
SwiftUI where the text's first baseline is, from the body font's
metrics, since SwiftUI takes a representable's baseline to be its top.
- The banner wraps and grows: it reports the height it laid out at the
width it was given, and the AppKit wrapper keeps a height constraint
from that report, so a narrow window makes it taller and pushes the
editor down. The hosting view's own intrinsic size is for an unbounded
width, one line per notice however narrow the window, and is switched
off.

## Checked

Ten tests on the parser, the resolver run with a stand-in script, the
fingerprint following pin files up the tree, and the cache asking the
resolver once and again only after a pin changes. In the built
application with the bundle changes linked in, a lone `.rb` beside a
`.ruby-version` pinned to an installed 4.0.7 ran on 4.0.7 where it ran
on the application's 4.0.9 before, and one beside a pin to an
uninstalled 3.3.0 ran on 4.0.9 with the notice above it, the path
showing its file in Finder. rv itself decides what a pin is:
`.ruby-version` beats `.tool-versions`, the home directory's pin stands
in for a project without one, and a `ruby` line in a Gemfile is not a
pin.

The bundle halves are textmate3/ruby.tmbundle #2, which prefers the
variable, and textmate3/runtimes-ruby.tmbundle #3, which names the pin
file in its answer.

commits.summary: Check for updates every hour on the alpha and beta channels and once a day on release (#89)
commits.body:
Sparkle checks on a schedule, not at launch: at launch it asks whether
the interval has passed since the last check, and if not it waits out
the remainder. The interval was Sparkle's default of a day for every
channel, so a copy on the alpha channel that had checked an hour before
an alpha landed would not ask again until the next day. A new build is
the point of being on a prerelease channel.

The interval now follows the channel: every hour on alpha and beta, once
a day on release. The application delegate sets it whenever the defaults
change, and only when the channel's interval differs from the one in
force, since Sparkle keeps the interval in the defaults and resets its
schedule on every set. Sparkle's header says to set the property only as
a user choice rather than on every launch, and the channel is that
choice. The Updates pane says which cadence the chosen channel has,
under the channel picker.

Checked on this machine with the alpha channel selected: the interval in
the defaults went from unset to 3600 at launch, and because the last
check was older than an hour, a check ran at once.

commits.summary: Drop the zero termination call that clang warns about in the temporary file template (#88)
commits.body:
The one warning in the build: `path.cc` called `str.c_str()` and threw
the result away, with a comment saying it ensured the buffer was zero
terminated. That was a C++03 habit. Since C++11 a `std::string` is zero
terminated at `size()` whether or not anything has asked for `c_str()`,
and `mkstemp` and `mkdtemp` write into the buffer below on that
guarantee. The call did nothing, and clang now says so, since `c_str` is
`nodiscard`.

The line is gone, with the guarantee stated where the call was. The io
tests pass and the compile is warning free.

commits.summary: Refresh the contributions data for 2.1.0-alpha.12
Stop the signing steps and one file browser object rerunning on every build (#87)
commits.body:
A build with nothing changed now does nothing. `ninja TextMate` twice in
a row ends in `ninja: no work to do`, and `ninja -n -d explain TextMate`
after a build lists nothing. Until now every build ran the eight signing
steps, the five nested ones and the eleven copies into the application
again, which is why every build ended in a dozen `replacing existing
signature` lines. Two causes, found with ninja's own explanation.

**The signing steps.** `codesign` rewrites the binary it signs, which is
the step's own input. Ninja 1.11 and later record a step's start time as
the time of its output unless the rule says `restat`, so the `.ok`
marker each signing step touches was on record as older than the binary
codesign had just rewritten, and the step was due again on the next run,
forever. The `Codesign` and `CodesignNested` rules now say `restat`, and
the marker's time on record is the marker's own, set by the touch after
codesign has finished. Two lines in `bin/rave`, each with the reason
beside it.

**One object in the file browser.** `SCMManager.mm` reached scm's driver
header through a symbolic link named `drivers` beside the file browser's
sources, there since 2018. That header's own `"../status.h"` was
recorded in the dependency file by its lexical path through the link,
`Frameworks/FileBrowser/src/drivers/../status.h`, which names no file,
so ninja found an input missing on every run and compiled the object
again, which relinked the framework, the application, and everything
signed after it. The duplicate `status.h` that #37 removed had been
masking this by existing at that lexical path. The link is gone and the
include names scm's source tree by a relative path, which both resolves
and records correctly. The drivers are scm's private API and not among
the headers it exports, which the comment says, and exporting them is a
separate question.

In Ruby terms, `bin/rave` is the Rakefile that writes `build.ninja`, and
the two signing rules are the two tasks whose side effect was to modify
their own prerequisite. Nothing else in the build changes, the scm tests
pass, and the application builds.

commits.summary: Show a notice when a .tm_properties section header cannot be read (#86)
commits.body:
A section header the parser cannot read opens a section that applies
nowhere, since #83, so the settings under it reach no file. The only
word of it was a line in the log. Now the notice strip above every
document window says which header, on which line of which file, could
not be read, and that its settings apply to nothing.

The settings code reports every parse of a settings file to a handler
the application installs, with the headers it could not read, an empty
list when all could. The application turns each into a notice keyed by
file and line, and clears every notice about a file before posting the
current ones, so fixing the file takes its notice down on the next read
without a dismissal. The handler runs on whatever thread asked for
settings, so the application hops to the main thread with its own copies
of the path and the list before touching the board.

Notices can carry a key now, which is what lets a poster replace or
clear what it said about one file. A keyed notice posted again with the
same text changes nothing and announces nothing. Plain notices are
untouched.

In the settings framework, in Ruby terms: the parser's malformed section
now remembers the header's text and line number, `parse_sections`
collects them into a list beside the sections it returns, and a module
level handler, set once by the application, receives the list after
every parse. The tests cover the two headers reported by text and line
and the clean file reported as empty, and the board's new keyed post and
prefix dismissal.

commits.summary: Wrap the key equivalents in the release notes in backticks (#84)
commits.body:
The HTML build dressed key equivalents such as ⌘S as keycaps through a
regex in `bin/gen_html`, and the native About window deliberately does
not, so since #71 they have read as plain glyphs. This wraps them in
backticks in `Changes.md` itself, once, so the renderer draws them as
code spans. The same regex's idea of a key equivalent, applied outside
the code spans and code blocks the file already has, and to no heading.
One change to it: the lone character after a modifier may not be a
bracket, so `[⌥]⌘V`, an optional modifier written in brackets, keeps its
brackets outside the span where the HTML had swallowed one.

148 lines changed, about 220 spans. A run of keys separated by slashes
or brackets becomes a span per key, `(`⇧`)`⌘⇠`/`⌘⇢``, which is what the
HTML did as well. The renderer's tests over the file, which read its
structure, pass unchanged, since a code span changes no block.

commits.summary: Accept a comma between the names of a .tm_properties section header (#83)
commits.body:
A section header separated its names with a semicolon and nothing else,
and a comma failed in one of two ways depending on the space after it.
`[*.md,*.markdown]` parsed as one glob that matched nothing. `[*.md,
*.markdown]` failed the header outright, the line was skipped, and the
settings under it fell into the section before, which for a header near
the top of a file is the root, so settings written for Markdown applied
to every file. The only sign was an error in the system log.

A comma now separates names the way a semicolon does. A comma inside
braces stays part of a glob, `tests/t_*.{cc,mm}`, and a comma inside
quotes stays part of a scope selector, which is why those two spellings
already worked and made the third look like it should. A header that
still cannot be read opens a section that applies nowhere, so what is
under it reaches no file rather than all of them, and the error naming
the line goes to the log as before. Two tests cover the four spellings
and the fallthrough.

commits.summary: Name the test a C++ test binary crashes in (#82)
commits.body:
The C++ test runner prints nothing on success and nothing on a crash.
`io_test` has died twice on continuous integration with exit 139 and no
other word, once in September and once this week, on pull requests that
touched nothing in io, and passed on rerun both times. Which test it was
is still unknown, which is the whole problem.

The runner installs a handler for the crashing signals that writes
`io_test: crashed in t_events::test_some_name` before letting the crash
go on, with only async signal safe calls. The running test is kept per
thread, since the tests run in parallel. The runner also prints one line
on success, `io_test: 45 tests passed`, so a run that printed nothing is
known to have crashed rather than passed, and `-v` names each test
before it runs.

Run one hundred and twenty times locally after this, sixty as continuous
integration runs it and sixty in parallel, `io_test` did not crash once.
The next time it does on the runner, the log will say where.

commits.summary: A Runtimes pane in Preferences (#81)
commits.body:
A pane between Bundles and Variables that shows where each runtime
stands. For Ruby and for Python: the bundle that carries the runtime and
whether it is installed, the version the application wants, the Ruby
directory or Python interpreter bundle commands run on now with a button
to show it in Finder, the manager behind it with its version and where
it was found, every version the manager has installed, and the newer
versions it could fetch.

Two actions. Install the bundle, through the catalog face the Bundles
pane already uses, after which the runtime is resolved as soon as the
bundle arrives. Install the wanted version when it is missing, which
asks the application to resolve the runtime again the way it does at
launch, through a notification the launch hook now listens for and
answers when it has settled. The versions are the application's to pin
and arrive with an update, so Newer is information and nothing switches
to it, and the pane says so in a line at the bottom.

The lists come from `rv ruby list --format json` and `uv python list
--managed-python --output-format json`, run off the main thread, from
the manager found the way the resolvers find it, the person's own first
and the bundle's last. Only final releases of the reference
implementation are listed. The parsing is pure functions with tests over
captured output from both managers.

On the way: the two bundle identifiers move from the launch hook into
`io/ruby_runtime.h` and `io/python_runtime.h`, where the pane can read
them too. `BundleCatalog` posts a notification on change beside the
single handler the Bundles pane owns. And rave's Swift test rule gains
the include directories the module compile has, since a module built
with a bridging header brings that header along with `@testable import`,
which the Preferences tests are the first to need.

Seen in light and dark with both bundles installed, Ruby 4.0.9 in use,
and Python showing the Install 3.14.9 button on a machine whose own uv
cannot fetch it.


This branch also carries the commit of #85, the Swift depfile fix in
rave, cherry picked so the pane builds on its own. Merge #85 first and
the duplicate falls away.

commits.summary: Give every Swift compile its own depfile and restat its outputs (#85)
commits.body:
Ninja treats `depfile` as a property of the rule, as it does
`description`, and rave wrote the depfile path on the shared
`CompileSwift` rule, so the rule carried whichever path rave wrote last,
the application's `TextMate.d`, and all 44 Swift compiles read that one
file. Every module recorded the application's dependencies as its own,
and a module the application imports, OakFoundation, then depended on
its own output. The moment that module needed rebuilding, ninja refused
every target with `dependency cycle: OakFoundation.swiftmodule ->
OakFoundation.swiftmodule`. Caught by building the two edges one at a
time from an empty database: OakFoundation's own compile recorded the
application's dependencies.

Each Swift edge sets `depfile_path` and the rule reads it, the same move
the module name made for the progress labels. The C++ rules were never
affected, since `$out.d` works for an edge with one output.

Found beside it: swiftc leaves an output alone when it would be
identical, so a source touched without a change left its object older
than the source for good, and every build recompiled every Swift module
and relinked the application. The Swift rules restat their outputs now,
so ninja records an unchanged output as current. After this, a real run
followed by a dry run wants no Swift step.

A build directory that recorded the wrong dependencies before this needs
`.ninja_deps` removed once, beside the `builddir` in `build.ninja`, and
rebuilds from there.

commits.summary: A notice strip above the text for what the launch did about the runtimes (#80)
commits.body:
When the application launches it asks the Runtimes bundles for the
pinned Ruby and Python, and the resolver may install one, stand in with
another version, or find none. Each of those went to the log, which
nobody reads, and the comment in the launch hook called them the
banner's material once the banner existed.

The banner is a strip above the text in every document window, in the
place the find bar appears, built as the Ruby runtime plan proposed.
`OakNoticeBoard` in OakAppKit holds the notices and announces each
change through the notification center. The launch hook posts to it:
`TextMate installed Ruby 4.0.9 for bundle commands, at …`, `Bundle
commands run on a Python other than 3.14.9. …`, `Ruby bundle commands
will not run. …`, with the resolver's own reason as the second sentence,
and the same text twice is one notice. `OakNoticeStripView` is a SwiftUI
strip hosted in an AppKit view the way the HTML output status bar is:
one row per notice in body text on a pale yellow, an info icon in amber
on light and the system yellow on dark, and a Dismiss button, and
`OakDocumentView` adds it to its top auxiliary views while the board has
anything and removes it when the board is empty. Dismissing removes the
notice from the board, so every window loses it together, a window
opened later shows what is still there, and the next launch starts
clean. The board has tests, and the strip was seen with a Python
fallback notice: a second window opened while it showed had it too, and
one Dismiss cleared both.

Not an alert, since nothing the person did caused it. Not a system
notification, since that asks permission on first launch for a message
most people see once. The `TM_RUBY` below minimum warning still goes to
a command's standard error, since the command framework does not reach
OakAppKit, and moving it onto the strip is a separate change.

commits.summary: Move Python to 3.14.9 (#79)
commits.body:
`.python-version` from 3.14.7 to 3.14.9, the current security patch
release, which is the one line pin since #78: `configure`, uv, and
`python_runtime::kPinnedVersion` all follow it, and the test that reads
the file passes against the build.

This merges only after the catalog serves the Runtimes Python bundle
with uv 0.13.5, the first uv that can download 3.14.9, since uv's list
of Pythons is compiled into its binary and a pin it cannot fetch would
fall back on every machine. The bundle's pull request is merged. The
CHANGELOG sentence from #78 that said Python stays at 3.14.7 now says
why it moved second.

commits.summary: Read the runtime pins from .ruby-version and .python-version, and move Ruby to 4.0.9 (#78)
commits.body:
The Ruby that bundle commands run on was `ruby_runtime::kPinnedVersion =
"4.0.6"`, a literal in C++, and the Python the same way at 3.14.7. The
build and the scripts had just gained `.ruby-version` for their own
Ruby, so there were two Ruby pins in two forms with nothing tying them,
and the one that reaches every user was three patches behind the release
that closed the vulnerabilities announced the day 4.0.8 came out.

Now there is one file per runtime. `.ruby-version` and the new
`.python-version`, the files rv and uv read natively, are captured by
the rave file the way `.macos-version` already is and handed to every
compile as `RUBY_RUNTIME_VERSION` and `PYTHON_RUNTIME_VERSION`, which
the two constants now are. Editing either file regenerates the build and
recompiles what carries the value. The developer's shell, `configure`,
continuous integration and the application all read the same line, and
moving a version is a one line diff of it.

The two tests that asserted the literals read the files instead and
compare them to what the build compiled in, plus that each has three
parts, so a stale build or a series pin would fail. Ruby moves from
4.0.6 to 4.0.9 with this. Python stays at 3.14.7.

commits.summary: Check the Ruby on the PATH against .ruby-version in configure (#76)
commits.body:
`.ruby-version` pins the Ruby the scripts run on, but `bin/rave` says
`#!/usr/bin/env ruby` and `configure` runs it directly, so the build has
run on whatever Ruby the PATH found with no check at all. `configure`
now reads the pin and refuses an older Ruby by name, the way it already
does for the SDK against `.macos-version` and Swift against
`.swift-version`. The refusal names the two ways rv provides the pinned
Ruby: `rv run sh ./configure` for one run, or `rv shell zsh` for the
PATH.

The comparison goes to the patch for all three, where it compared major
and minor. A patch release can be the one that closes a vulnerability,
as 4.0.9 did the day 4.0.8 came out, so a pin means what it says all the
way down. A missing part counts as zero, so `27.0` is `27.0.0`.

Tried: with the pin at 99.0, refused. On a shell whose PATH finds rv's
home pinned 4.0.7 against the repository's 4.0.9, refused with the
message above. Through `rv run sh ./configure`, 4.0.9, passes. The
eleven pair matrix in the helper's terms: 4.0.10, 4.1, 5, 6.10 against
6.4, 27.1 pass, and 4.0.7, 4.0, 6.3.9 against 6.4, 26.9 against 27.0 are
refused.

commits.summary: Delete the Title lines from the About pages and the code that skipped them (#77)
commits.body:
`Changes.md` and `Legal.md` opened with a MultiMarkdown `Title:` line
that fed the `<title>` tag of the HTML build. Neither goes through that
build anymore: they ship as Markdown and render natively, and the two
remaining readers of `Changes.md`, the version capture in the rave file
and the release script, look only for the newest release heading. The
two lines go, and with them the code in `MarkdownDocument` that skipped
such a block, its test, and the block in the fixture. Nothing the
renderer draws carries one.

The release notes digest changes once, so the Changes page shows itself
once after the next update, which is also correct, since the file
changed.

commits.summary: Name the Swift module in ninja's progress line (#75)
commits.body:
Every Swift compile shares one ninja rule, `CompileSwift`, and in ninja
a description belongs to the rule, not the step. So every Swift step
printed whichever description rave had written last, `Compile Swift
tests ‘SoftwareUpdateTests’` four times while compiling OakFoundation,
OakAppKit, BundlesManager and its tests. The work was right and the
label was not.

The rule's description now reads `Compile Swift ‘$module’…` and each
step sets `module` to its own name, which is what ninja provides for
exactly this. A rebuild prints `Compile Swift ‘OakFoundation’` and
`Compile Swift ‘OakFoundationTests’`.

commits.summary: Refresh the contributions data from the release scripts (#74)
commits.body:
The Contributions page's data is only as current as the last run of
`script/update_contributions`, and nothing ran it. The release scripts
now do, between their preconditions and the build: the script reads
`main` and asks GitHub about the commits since the last run through the
`gh` the preconditions already require, and when the data changed it is
committed as `Refresh the contributions data for <version>` and pushed,
so the build number counts that commit and the released application
carries every commit on `main` but the refresh itself.

Between releases the data is as current as the last release, which is
fine, since nobody sees the page of a build that was not released. Not
the build, which stays offline and token free, and not a CI workflow,
which would put a bot commit after every merge.

commits.summary: Say what multimarkdown is for now that the release notes are native: the Help pages
Refresh the contributions data after #72 (#73)
commits.body:
`script/update_contributions` run on `main` after #72 merged. The four
commits of that branch leave the data, since they are not in `main`'s
history, and the squash merge takes their place with its account from
GitHub.

The script now logs `main` rather than `HEAD`, so the data is `main`'s
history wherever the script is run from. Run on this branch after the
change, it wrote the same bytes.

commits.summary: Show Contributions natively, with the data behind it as one JSON file per year (#72)
commits.body:
The About window's Contributions page was the last one in a web view.
Its HTML was made at build time by an ERB template inside
`Contributions.md`, running `git log` over the checkout, hashing author
emails for Gravatar, looking up GitHub accounts in a hand kept table of
forty email hashes that stops in 2014, leaving out Allan Odgaard's
commits by a joke of his own, and linking every commit to the upstream
repository.

**The data.** `script/update_contributions` writes one JSON file per
year under the application's resources with every commit's hash, author
date, author name, summary and body, and the GitHub username and avatar
that GitHub itself resolves the author to through the repository's
commits endpoint, which works for private emails too. Each year is
sorted by author date, newest first, since `git log`'s own order follows
commit date and parentage and a rebase or a cherry pick puts the two out
of step. The files are committed, so a build needs neither the network
nor a token. Commits already in the files keep what they have, so a
routine run asks GitHub about the commits since the last one and reads
one page. A commit GitHub has not seen, one on a branch that has not
merged, takes the account of another commit by the same email. 6,071
commits in eleven files. Allan's 5,171 are in. 39 commits have no
account, all old, one of them because its author email is empty, which
the API answers with an empty object rather than null.

**The page.** `Contribution` and `ContributionYear` in OakFoundation
decode the files, with tests over a real year file, and
`days(calendar:)` groups a year by the day each commit was authored,
under the titles the page used. `ContributionsView` reads the directory
off the main thread behind a progress indicator and lists every commit
under a heading per day: the author's avatar, the summary with a chevron
that opens the rest of the message drawn as Markdown so its wrapped
lines read as paragraphs, the short hash linked to the commit in this
repository, and the author linked to their profile as name and username
when GitHub knows them. `MarkdownBlocksView` in OakAppKit is the
renderer without its scroll view, for a body inside a row that already
scrolls.

**What leaves.** The web view, the bridge script, the message handler,
`Contributions.md` with its stylesheet and script, and
`bin/gen_credits.rb`. The Markdown to HTML build stays, since the Help
pages are converted by it.

**Dependencies.** `gh` is what the script asks GitHub through, and it
was not declared anywhere, so it is in the Brewfile and the README now,
and the script aborts naming them when it is missing or signed out. The
same check found `rv` and `swiftlint` undeclared, so they are declared
too, and `.ruby-version` pins the Ruby the scripts run on, which until
now came from the machine's home directory.

commits.summary: Show the About window's Changes, Legal and Bundles pages natively (#71)
commits.body:
Three of the About window's five pages leave the web view, using the
renderer from #70.

Changes and Legal were Markdown converted to HTML at build time by
`bin/gen_html` around `multimarkdown` and shown in a `WKWebView`. They
are now the same Markdown, shipped as Markdown through a rave `copy` so
the `files` conversion does not touch them, parsed by Foundation and
drawn in SwiftUI through `OakMarkdownPageViewController`, which the
Objective-C window creates by file URL and takes the view of. A file
that will not read or parse shows the reason in its place. The release
notes shown after an update are this page, and the digest that decides
whether to show them is taken over the Markdown now.

Bundles was an HTML page filled by JavaScript with each installed
bundle's `Changes.json`. It is now `BundleChanges`, one file decoded,
and `BundleChangesLog`, every installed bundle's commits mixed newest
first and grouped by month, keeping this year and the two before, drawn
by `BundleChangesView` as a list with a heading per month and a commit's
body behind a disclosure. The window hands `BundleChangesViewController`
the file URLs and nothing else, and makes a new one each time the page
is shown so a bundle installed since the last look is in the list. The
model has tests over two real `Changes.json` files, with the year and
calendar passed in so the grouping is the same on any day.

The About page was native already. `About.md` was still being converted
and shipped with nothing reading it, and goes, along with `Bundles.html`
and the `TextMate.version` and `.copyright` bridge variables that only
`About.md` used. Contributions stays in the web view, with the bridge
script for its error logging, until its layout is redesigned, and
`gen_html` and the templates stay for it alone.

Key equivalents such as ⌘S read as plain glyphs. The HTML had dressed
them as keycaps through a regex that also misplaced brackets, and the
native pages deliberately do not. Looks are a first pass from the
stylesheet's sizes, and sprucing them up is a separate pull request.

commits.summary: Add a native Markdown renderer to OakAppKit (#70)
commits.body:
The About window renders its Changes and Legal pages by converting
Markdown to HTML at build time and showing it in a web view. Neither
page has a content design concern that needs HTML, so this is the
renderer that lets them be native, ahead of the window change that uses
it.

`MarkdownDocument` is the model. Foundation parses the Markdown with
full interpretation, which keeps block structure as presentation intents
on the runs of one attributed string, innermost first with an identity
per block. A recursive descent over those runs recovers headings,
paragraphs, bullet lists that nest, and indented code blocks, with each
list item carrying blocks of its own, which is how an item holds a
second paragraph or a code block. Each run keeps its inline attributes,
links, code spans and emphasis, for `Text` to draw. The MultiMarkdown
metadata block at the top of each About page, `Title:` on all of them
and `CSS:` and `JS:` on Contributions, is skipped under MultiMarkdown's
own rule, since the HTML build still reads it for the one tab that stays
on HTML.

`MarkdownView` walks the blocks in a lazy stack inside a scroll view.
Headings take the large title, title and title3 fonts, which is roughly
where the HTML stylesheet's sizes landed. Bullets are a glyph beside a
stack of the item's blocks, so nesting is the view inside itself. Code
blocks are monospaced on a quiet background. Links open through the
environment's `openURL`. Key equivalents such as ⌘S draw as the plain
glyphs they are in the Markdown. The HTML build dressed them as keycaps
through a regex, and that styling is deliberately not reproduced.

Tests cover the model: a fixture with every construct the About pages
use, asserted exactly, and the real `Changes.md`, asserted structurally
so the test survives each release. Nothing uses the view yet. The window
change follows as its own pull request, and no package is taken:
Foundation's parser does what these pages need.

commits.summary: Refresh the seed bundles with unescaped Changes.json (#69)
commits.body:
The fifteen seed bundles the application ships for a first launch carry
a `Changes.json` each, built by the catalog before #68 and
textmate3/api.textmate3.com#4 stopped HTML-escaping commit messages into
it. The catalog archives are rebuilt and published with the clean text,
and this repacks the seeds from them with `script/update_seed_bundles`,
so the Bundles tab shows an apostrophe rather than `'` before the
first catalog refresh too. Archives only, no code.

commits.summary: Insert commit summaries and bodies into the Bundles page as text (#68)
commits.body:
The Bundles tab of the About window builds its list from each installed
bundle's `Changes.json`. The page already inserted the bundle name and
the author as text nodes, but put the commit summary and body in through
`innerHTML`. That one choice is why the catalog HTML-escapes those two
fields when it writes the file, so the data carries `TextMate's`
where the commit said `TextMate's`.

This makes the two fields text nodes like the others. A companion change
in the catalog stops the escaping. Order matters a little: this page
lands first, since a page using `innerHTML` on unescaped text is the one
combination that actually misrenders.

Bundles already installed carry escaped files until the archives are
rebuilt and refreshed, so for that stretch the tab shows `'`
literally where it showed an apostrophe. That is the whole cost, and it
clears with the next catalog build.

commits.summary: Raise the minimum macOS to 27 (and Swift to 6.4) (#67)
commits.body:
The floor moves from macOS 26 to 27, the current system. The step to 26
was taken expecting this one: the floor at first release should be the
current macOS, so the application carries no availability guards and no
reasoning about which system has what. The first release has not
happened yet, and the machine this is built on runs 27.0.1, so the two
things that deferred it are gone. Nothing in the open work requires 27,
and I would rather that be on record than have it reconstructed later as
a technical necessity.

**The commits.** The first is a refactor with no behavior change: the
release script restated the minimum in a constant of its own,
`MINIMUM_MACOS`, separately from `APP_MIN_OS` in `default.rave`, so the
two could drift and the update feed could claim a different floor from
the application. It now reads the value from `default.rave` the way it
already reads the feed key and feed URL. The second is the raise itself:
`APP_MIN_OS` to `27.0`, from which every compiler, linker, asset catalog
and `Info.plist` value derives, plus the README, the release notes and
the changelog. The rest move continuous integration to the macOS 27
image, correct what I had written about it, and name the Swift toolchain
the build needs, below.

**What a clean rebuild at 27 surfaced.** Nothing. 894 steps from an
empty build directory, no deprecations, no errors. The one warning is a
bare `str.c_str()` in `io/path.cc`, kept by its own comment as a
null-termination superstition, which libc++ flags as `nodiscard` at any
deployment target. It is old code meeting a new compiler, not the floor,
and it belongs to the housekeeping sweep rather than here. The built
application reports `LSMinimumSystemVersion 27.0`, and the main binary
and `mate` both carry `minos 27.0` against the 27.0 SDK.

**What it costs.** Everyone on macOS 26, which is most Macs today and
still supported. The largest cohort any step has excluded, accepted on
the same basis as the step to 26.
