**Continuous integration, and two things I got wrong on the way.** The
workflow now runs on `xcode-27`, GitHub's macOS 27 image: 27.0.1 with
Xcode 27 and the 27 SDK, in preview, so the runner sees the same system
and headers a developer does. I had first written that no 27 image
existed and that a binary built for 27 could not launch on the 26 one.
Both were wrong. The image exists under GitHub's Xcode naming, which I
had not searched for. And the loader does not refuse a binary whose
minimum is newer than the running system. A throwaway test program built
with a minimum of 28.0, a version that does not exist, so that it was
certainly newer than the 27.0.1 it ran on, ran without complaint. So the
26 image had already built and run every suite at the 27 floor, lacking
only the 27 SDK. That finding is kept in the changelog because it is
true and useful. The `ci.yml` comment says where to move when a
`macos-27` label appears.



**The two versions the build needs are named in two files.** Until this
branch no toolchain version was stated anywhere: `-swift-version 6` is a
language mode, the compiler was whatever the selected Xcode had, and the
deployment target sat on line one of `default.rave`. Now
`.macos-version` holds the deployment target and `.swift-version` the
Swift, both at the top of the tree.

`default.rave` reads the floor from `.macos-version` through a
`capture`, named by a `${dir}` path so rave tracks the file: editing it
regenerates the build, and every flag that carries the floor rebuilds
with it. The release script reads the same file for the minimum it
writes into the update feed, so the feed cannot name a different floor
from the application it points at.

`configure` checks both before anything else runs: the SDK the selected
Xcode carries against `.macos-version`, and `swiftc --version` against
`.swift-version`. An older Xcode used to fail deep in the build on a
missing SDK with an error that named neither. Both refusals now say
which file, which version it found, and which Xcode provides what is
needed. Versions compare as numbers, major then minor, so 6.10 is newer
than 6.4.

swiftly, the toolchain manager that reads `.swift-version`, is in the
Brewfile, so `swiftly install` fetches the Swift it names. The build
itself still compiles with the Swift of the selected Xcode through
`xcrun`, because that is where the SDK is, and that is the one
`configure` checks.

commits.summary: Mark CommitMessageDocument @MainActor (#66)
commits.body:
The build compiled clean but with three actor isolation warnings:
`CommitMessageDocument` held and called into `CommitMessageView`, an
`NSView` subclass whose isolation is inferred from `NSView` itself,
without being isolated to the same actor.

The class is only ever touched from SwiftUI's own main-actor context, so
`@MainActor` states what was already true rather than changing behavior.
Full rebuild is warning free.

commits.summary: Move the chooser abbreviation memory to Swift (#65)
commits.body:
The first piece of the highest ranked Swift candidate, and the one that
is model rather than view: what a person picked the last time they typed
a given abbreviation, which is what puts a previously chosen file ahead
of whatever the ranker would have offered. Go to File, the symbol
chooser, the bundle item chooser and Favorites all keep one, under their
own names, and it is read on every keystroke.

**Two bugs, both from the same decision.** The list was trimmed to fifty
and written to user defaults only in response to
`NSApplicationWillTerminate`, and from `dealloc`. So it grew without
limit for as long as the application ran, with every keystroke searching
all of it, and quitting any way other than by choosing Quit wrote
nothing at all. A pick is trimmed and saved when it is made now.

**One behavior clarified rather than changed.** An empty abbreviation
answered an empty list, because the guard happened to return the array
it had been about to fill. Every remembered pick has an empty prefix, so
without that guard the whole list would go in front of the ranker. It is
now a stated rule with a test rather than an accident of where a
variable was declared.

**The name and the stored format are unchanged.**
`@objc(OakAbbreviations)`, the same two selectors, and the same `short`
and `long` keys in user defaults, so nobody loses what they had and the
three call sites change one import.

**What is left of this candidate.** The three choosers themselves and
the table view they share, 2,300 lines, which is a SwiftUI window and
wants its own pull request. The ranker stays in C++ behind a face, as
the plan says.

**Tests.** Thirteen, over ordering, the prefix rule, the trimming, the
round trip through defaults, and a malformed entry being ignored rather
than crashing.

commits.summary: Move the commit window to Swift and SwiftUI (#63)
commits.body:
The first of the ranked Swift candidates, taken because it is the most
contained: a standalone tool with a window, launched by bundle commands,
that no framework of the application depends on.

**What it draws is unchanged.** The message field is still TextMate's
own editor, so it still highlights with the commit grammar the source
control system asks for and still runs bundle items. The file list still
hides and shows, and remembers which. The action menu, the diff button,
the previous messages, the option key turning Commit into Commit and
Continue: all the same.

**What is gone is how it was drawn.** Showing or hiding the file list
rebuilt about three hundred lines of Auto Layout by hand, tearing down
the table, unbinding it, removing and recreating the document view's
height constraint four times per toggle, and running the animation
through a constraint whose constant was being animated while the
constraint itself was replaced. That is one `if` in a `VStack` now.

The status letters were built as an attributed string, one letter at a
time, padded with hair spaces and given an `NSExpansionAttributeName`
computed with `logf` so each cell reached thirteen points. A monospaced
font in a fixed frame does that without arithmetic.

**What stayed Objective-C++, and why.** The socket listener, because it
deals in file descriptors and a C++ callback registry.
`CommitMessageView`, a plain Objective-C face over `OakDocumentView`,
because that header reaches Objective-C++ and the Swift compiler reads
plain Objective-C only. `CommitWindowBridge`, the same for `io::exec`,
`path::escape` and `format_string::expand`. Both faces are narrow and
are what the Swift sees.

**Three bugs the port found.** Each is covered by a test.

Paths and statuses were paired by indexing the statuses array with the
path's position, so a caller passing more paths than statuses raised an
exception and took the window with it. They are zipped now, and an
unmatched path is dropped.

An option given without a value called `cancel:` in the middle of
parsing, which sent the reply and then carried on parsing. It now drops
the option.

`if(actions != nil | [actions count] != 0)` used a bitwise or on a
pointer and a count, so it was always true. It is gone rather than
fixed, because nothing needed the condition.

**Tests, which this had none of.** 35 of them, over what the window
decides rather than what it draws: reading the tool's arguments, which
files start checked and why, what the commit button says, the shell
quoting of a message containing an apostrophe, and the commit message
history.

commits.summary: Move the HTML output status strip to SwiftUI (#64)
commits.body:
Part of the second ranked Swift candidate. This takes the status strip,
which is the piece of it that is plainly a view and nothing else.

**What it replaces.** `HOStatusBar` chose between a spinner and a
progress bar by adding one `NSProgressIndicator` to the view hierarchy,
removing the other, and rebuilding its own constraints from visual
format strings every time. Which of the two was showing could therefore
only be answered by looking at a window. It is a property now,
`showsSpinner`, and it has tests.

**Nothing around it changed.** `HOBrowserView` still owns the strip,
still lays it out under the web view, and still sets the same five
properties by name. The Swift class keeps the name `HOStatusBar` through
`@objc`, so Objective-C++ sees what it always did.

One property was renamed. `busy`, with a getter of `isBusy`, becomes
`isBusy` outright, because Swift cannot give a property a getter name
that disagrees with its setter without renaming both.
`HOJSBridgeDelegate` and its two callers moved with it.

**What is still Objective-C++ in this framework, and why.** The web view
host, the scheme handler that streams a file handle, the JavaScript
bridge and the auto scroll helper. Those deal in `std::map`
environments, WebKit delegate plumbing and a `WKURLSchemeHandler`, and
none of them is a view. They are the rest of this candidate rather than
something skipped, and they want their own pull request.

**Tests.** Six, over what the strip decides and over the five properties
the Objective-C++ sets by name, since renaming one of those would
compile and then quietly do nothing.

This carries the same `bin/rave` change as the commit window port, which
lets a Swift test reach its module. The two branches are independent, so
whichever lands first makes the other's copy a no-op.

commits.summary: Refresh the seed bundles after the Python work landed (#62)
commits.body:
The archives in `Resources/SeedBundles` are built from the bundle
checkouts, so they still carried the Python 2 versions of Bundle Support
and Markdown after those bundles moved to Python 3. Rebuilt from each
bundle's `main`.

Bundle Support no longer ships its vendored copy of `plistlib`, and
Markdown ships the maintained html2text rather than the 2008 one. Every
other archive moved only because the catalog's tar now excludes
`__pycache__` and `.DS_Store`.

commits.summary: A runtime bundle per language, and a Python for bundle commands (#58)
commits.body:
A spike, not a finished decision. Paired with a draft in the Runtimes
bundle that adds the resolver this reads.

The Ruby a bundle command runs on is already settled: the application
names a version, a mandatory bundle carries the manager, a resolver
answers on standard output, and the system runtime is never used. Python
gets the same shape with uv in place of rv. This is an addition. Nothing
about Ruby changes behavior.

Python is in worse shape than Ruby was. Fourteen bundles run it across
fifty files, macOS ships 3.9.6 at `/usr/bin/python3`, and since macOS
12.3 there is nothing at all at `/usr/bin/python`, so a `#!/usr/bin/env
python` command does not run at all rather than running on something
old.

Two commits, the refactor kept apart from the addition.

**The refactor.** Reading a resolver's answer is the same work whatever
the language, so it moves to `runtime_resolver`, which takes the keyword
as an argument. `ruby_runtime` keeps every signature and field name it
had and delegates, so nothing that calls it changed. Its test file is
untouched and still passes.

**The addition.** `python_runtime` beside it, `TM_PYTHON` and
`TM_APPLICATION_PYTHON` in the basic environment, the interpreter's
directory on `PATH`, a launch hook that asks the bundle for a Python off
the main thread, and the shebang rewrite extended.

Two things Python needs that Ruby did not.

The answer is an interpreter rather than a directory, because `uv python
find` answers that way and a Python's layout varies more than a Ruby's.

The system Python has to be excluded on purpose. rv does not know the
system Ruby, so the Ruby resolver could never answer with it by
accident. uv finds `/usr/bin/python3` and Xcode's copy readily, so the
resolver passes `--managed-python` and `is_system_python` refuses those
paths plus the Command Line Tools and the system framework wherever a
person names one.

The shebang rewrite now handles both languages through one function. A
command is rewritten for one language only, and the interpreter is
looked up after the pattern matches rather than before, so a Python
command never triggers a warning about a `TM_RUBY` the person set.

**The pin.** `kPinnedVersion` is `3.14.7`, the latest CPython, spelled
exactly the way Ruby's `4.0.6` is and for the same reason: a series
would move under the bundles without anything recording that it moved.
Moving it is a decision, and the test asserting the constant is what
makes that decision show up in a diff.

**Also not done.** The uv binary is not vendored into the bundle, so
this works only where uv is already installed. Vendoring it is a signing
and size question the rv vendoring had to answer once and should answer
again deliberately.



**Every runnable Python file in every bundle is now Python 3**, across
fourteen bundle pull requests opened beside this one, with tests in four
bundles that had none. So the Python this finds has something to run.


---

## The runtimes are one bundle per language now

| Bundle | Install | Tarball | Carries |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Runtimes | mandatory, seeded | 4.6 KB | the protocol every resolver
answers in, and `script/vendor` |
| Runtimes Ruby | mandatory, seeded | 5.3 MB | `rv`, and the Ruby bundle
commands run on |
| Runtimes Python | optional | 14 MB | `uv`, and the Python bundle
commands run on |

Ruby stays mandatory, because every bundle's support library is Ruby and
an application without it is one where most commands fail. Python is
optional, because a minority of bundles run Python and `uv` is larger
than everything else TextMate ships put together.

**Optional is what made vendoring `uv` affordable.** Measured rather
than guessed: it takes the bundle's tarball from 5.3 MB to 20 MB,
against a whole application download of 21.8 MB, and Sparkle ships full
archives here rather than deltas so that would be paid on every update
by everyone. Behind a choice, it is paid once by the people who want it,
and the seed set stays exactly 8.6 MB. The alternative, fetching `uv` at
runtime, would have reinvented signature checking, progress and consent,
all of which bundle install already does.

**A command that needs a language with no runtime behind it now says
which bundle provides it**, rather than referring to a log. It still
fails, because it must not reach the system interpreter, but its error
names the bundle and where to install it. It also posts
`OakRuntimeMissingNotification`, and the application offers the install
once per launch per language. The command does not wait on that, so
nothing depends on the offer being seen or answered.

**Not being installed is not an error.** A machine whose owner writes no
Python is the ordinary case, so nothing is logged about it at launch. A
Python command actually running is what asks.

`BundlesManager` gained `bundleForIdentifier:`, which is how the offer
finds the bundle to install.

commits.summary: Refuse a TM_RUBY that is not an executable file and say why (#57)
commits.body:
I swapped my Ruby manager and every Ruby bundle command stopped working,
⌘R included. The cause was a `TM_RUBY` in my `.tm_properties` still
naming the old manager's path, which no longer exists.

Nothing checked that. `ruby_for_shebang` already refuses a `TM_RUBY`
naming the system Ruby and warns when one is below the 4.0 minimum, but
a path with nothing at it was passed straight into the command's
shebang. `posix_spawn` then failed with `ENOENT`, and the error names
the script being spawned rather than the interpreter that is missing, so
it reads as a missing script and sends you looking at the wrong file.
From a Finder launch there is no message at all.

Now a `TM_RUBY` that is not an executable file is refused the same way
the system Ruby is. Commands run on `TM_APPLICATION_RUBY`, the version
the application pins, and the reason is said on standard error for a
launch from a terminal and in the log for every other launch. The two
refusals share one function, so they word themselves alike and both
reach both places.

The tests needed reworking. They asserted that a `TM_RUBY` was honored
using plausible but fictional paths such as
`/opt/rubies/ruby-4.0.6/bin/ruby`, which only passed because nothing
checked. Every case that expects a `TM_RUBY` honored now creates a real
file in a jail, a link to a binary, since nothing here runs it. The
fictional path keeps its place in the cases that expect a refusal, which
is what it always was.

Three cases are added: a missing `TM_RUBY` falling back to the
application's, a `TM_RUBY` naming a directory refused the same way, and
a missing `TM_RUBY` with no fallback declining to run rather than
reaching the system Ruby.

commits.summary: Refresh the seed bundles from the current catalog archives
Write out the grapheme loops that used the citerate macro (#56)
commits.body:
The fourth piece of the iteration macros, after #53, #54 and #55.
`citerate(ch, expression)` held the expression in a hidden temporary and
walked it, and every one of its sixteen uses walks the graphemes of a
string through `diacritics::make_range`.

Four of them only look at each code point, so they are a range for over
the range, which one loop in the layout already was. The other twelve
ask the iterator for the grapheme's bytes and length, so the range gets
a name, `graphemes`, and the loop walks its iterators in plain code.

Behavior is unchanged at every site. With this the header
`oak/iterator_macros.h` has no callers left. Deleting it touches the
same lines as the three earlier pieces, so it waits for them to merge
and is its own small pull request after.

commits.summary: Write out the loops that used the foreach macro over an iterator pair (#55)
commits.body:
The third piece of the iteration macros, after #53 and #54. `foreach(it,
first, last)` hid a `for` over an iterator pair. Its twenty eight uses
are written out as that loop, with the end named `last`, or `stop` where
`last` is already the name of a parameter.

Every one of them walks a slice of a sorted structure, `lower_bound` to
`upper_bound`, or a run of UTF-8 through the utf8 iterator, so a range
for has no range to take and the iterator pair stays. One site, the
bundle query cache, had its end condition on the same line as a comment
about why the end is what it is, and that now reads as a named local
above the loop.

The macro itself stays in the header for now, since `citerate` is built
on it. That is the last piece, and the header goes with it.

Behavior is unchanged at every site.

commits.summary: Write out the loops that used the iterate macro and delete it (#54)
commits.body:
The second piece of the iteration macros, after #53. `iterate(it,
container)` hid a `for` over `std::begin` and `std::end`. Its sixteen
uses are written out.

One becomes a range for, the tab size update over the layout's rows,
because it only reads each row. The other fifteen keep the iterator,
because they need it: erasing from the container, returning the
iterator, pushing it onto a list, measuring its distance from the start,
or stepping it inside the body. Those are the same loop the macro
expanded to, spelled out.

The macro is deleted. Behavior is unchanged at every site.

commits.summary: Walk containers backwards with std::views::reverse in place of the riterate macro (#53)
commits.body:
The first piece of the iteration macros in `oak/iterator_macros.h`.
`riterate(it, container)` walked a container backwards through reverse
iterators, and its fourteen uses all read the element and nothing else,
so each becomes a range for over `std::views::reverse` with the element
named for what it is: a line, a record, a mark, a rule.

One exception is the test over the basic tree, which is not a standard
range, so it walks `rbegin` to `rend` in plain code. The macro is
deleted, and the prelude gains the ranges header.

Behavior is unchanged at every site. The remaining macros, `foreach`,
`iterate` and `citerate`, are separate pieces, since many of their uses
need the iterator itself and each site needs its own reading.

commits.summary: Say once when TM_RUBY is below the 4.0 minimum (#52)
commits.body:
A `TM_RUBY` below the minimum is honored. Nothing said so, so a bundle
command failing on Ruby 3 read as a bundle bug.

Now, the first time a command runs on a given `TM_RUBY`, that Ruby is
asked its version and, when it is below 4.0, one line goes to the
application's standard error naming the Ruby, its version, the minimum,
and that a failure may be the version rather than the bundle. The answer
is kept for the life of the process, so each path is asked once and said
once. The system Ruby refusal on the same path already spoke this way,
so the two read alike.

The minimum, `4.0`, lives beside the pinned version in the io framework,
with `is_below_minimum` comparing major then minor as numbers and
`version_of` asking a Ruby through `-e`. Both have tests, the latter
against a stand in script that answers 3.2.1 whatever it is asked.

Left where it is: the warning reaches standard error, not the person.
The launch banner that would carry it does not exist yet, and where that
banner goes is a design choice worth making once.

commits.summary: Test end to end that a Ruby command runs on the Ruby its shebang names (#51)
commits.body:
The shebang tests in `t_shebang.cc` check the text the runner produces.
Nothing checked that the kernel then honors it. These tests run a Ruby
command through the real runner, the way the application does, and look
at what comes back.

- With `TM_RUBY` naming a stand in Ruby, a link to `echo` in a temporary
directory, the command's output is the script's path, which the runner
reports as the command's name. The stand in ignores the command's own
text, so that line can only have come from the kernel running what the
rewritten shebang named. It has to be a binary: the kernel refuses a
script as another script's interpreter, which the first version of this
test learned on the runner.
- With no `TM_RUBY` and `TM_APPLICATION_RUBY` naming the stand in, a
`#!/usr/bin/ruby` command lands on it too.
- With a real Ruby on the machine that is not the system's, found where
rv, chruby or Homebrew put theirs, `RUBY_VERSION` printed by the command
equals what that Ruby prints when asked directly. Without such a Ruby
the test says so on standard error and checks nothing, rather than reach
for the system Ruby.
- With `TM_RUBY` naming the system Ruby and no other Ruby known, the
command does not run: exit status 1, no output, and the message on
standard error saying there is no Ruby.

The test helper that runs a command gains a way to set or remove
variables, so a test can take away what the application would have set.

commits.summary: Order version strings with a Swift Version (#50)
commits.body:
`OakCompareVersionStrings` ordered version strings by hand in C++ behind
an Objective-C function: components as numbers, a hyphen prerelease
before the release, plus build metadata ignored, trailing zero groups
ignored, a missing string before everything. Semantic Versioning
precedence, plus the loose forms that turn up in a catalog field and a
`mate --version` line.

It is a Swift `Version` now, `Comparable`, the first Swift in the
SoftwareUpdate framework. The same rules, token for token, with one
difference: numeric components compare by their digits rather than
through an integer, so a number too large for one orders instead of
failing. The two Objective-C callers, the catalog's minimum application
version check and the check for an older installed `mate`, ask through
an `OakVersion` face.

The test table moves to Swift Testing, the exhaustive pairwise table
included, and the old Objective-C test file goes. The framework's test
target is Swift only now, the way rave already handles for BundleSchema.

I looked at taking a package for this and decided against it. Two are
maintained, but the build does not consume Swift packages, one rejects
the loose forms the callers pass, and Sparkle's own comparator does not
know prerelease from release. Eighty lines of Swift with the existing
tests was the smaller move.

commits.summary: Rewrite shebangs that spell out the system framework Ruby (#49)
commits.body:
The shebang rewrite that points Ruby commands at the pinned Ruby knew
two spellings, `#!/usr/bin/env ruby` and `#!/usr/bin/ruby`. A dozen
commands in the experimental, terminalmate and wikidot bundles spell out
a third:
`#!/System/Library/Frameworks/Ruby.framework/Versions/1.8/usr/bin/ruby`.
Those went untouched, straight to a Ruby 1.8 path that current macOS
does not have, so they failed before their first line ran.

The pattern now matches the framework path with any version directory,
and the four cases are tested: a plain one, one with flags, one with the
trailing space one of the bundle commands carries, and one with no Ruby
known at all, which refuses to run like the other spellings do.

The bundles get the same fix at the source, since a shebang naming the
system Ruby is a bundle bug. Those are separate pull requests in the
three bundle repositories.

commits.summary: Drop the CFPlugInCOM import the QuickLook generator needed (#47)
commits.body:
The Objective-C prelude imports `CFPlugInCOM.h` with a comment saying it
must come before `QuickLook.h`. That ordering served the QuickLook
generator, which was built on the CFPlugIn COM interface. The generator
is gone, and the current SDK's QuickLook headers include what they need
themselves, so the line has nothing left to precede.

The Quartz umbrella on the next line stays. It is how `QLPreviewPanel`
reaches the file browser's Quick Look panel, and its comment now says so
instead of pointing at a private header.

A change to the prelude rebuilds everything, which is the test.

commits.summary: Silence the frozen string warning in gen_test (#48)
commits.body:
Every test binary build prints a warning from `bin/gen_test` under Ruby 4.0: a literal string will be frozen in the future. The script starts the generated source as a string literal and appends to it, which is the mutation the warning is about.

The literal becomes `String.new`, which is mutable by definition, and the warning is gone. Nothing else changes, and the generated test runner is byte for byte the same. No CHANGELOG line, since the application is untouched.

commits.summary: Tell GitHub the headers are Objective-C++, not C (#46)
commits.body:
GitHub's language bar lists 21 files as C. They are the headers, which
linguist counts as C when it cannot tell, and every one of them is
Objective-C++ or C++.

A one line `.gitattributes` tells linguist what they are. Nothing in the
build reads the file. No CHANGELOG line, since nothing about the
application changes.

commits.summary: Fold environment maps with insert at each site and drop oak/algorithm.h (#45)
commits.body:
The last piece of taking `oak/algorithm.h` apart, after #40, #41, #42,
#43 and #44.

What was left was a `<<` operator on two maps. It folded one set of
environment variables into another, leaving any variable already set as
it was, and it read like stream output. It was also the one thing in the
header that lived outside the `oak` namespace, so every file that saw
`std::map` saw it.

The eleven places that fold environments now say it with the map's own
`insert`, each with a named local for the variables being folded in. The
order of folding, and so which value wins when two sets name the same
variable, is unchanged at every site. One of them, in the completion
code, chained three folds on one line and is now three locals and three
inserts.

With that the header is empty, so it is deleted, along with its line in
the oak umbrella header and the four files that included it directly for
helpers that had already left.

commits.summary: Write the family removal of marks out at its two callers (#44)
commits.body:
The fifth piece of taking `oak/algorithm.h` apart, after #40, #41, #42
and #43.

`oak::erase_descendent_keys` removed a family of mark types from a
sorted map: given `error/`, every key under it. Two places call it, the
buffer's marks and the document's store of marks for files that are not
open. Nothing else in the application has that shape, so it was not a
general algorithm, it was marks logic living in a header every source
file sees.

The loop is written out at both callers, five lines each with a comment
saying why the map's order makes it work. Two copies of five plain lines
read better than one template reached through the oak umbrella.

The buffer's marks had no tests. This adds three: removing one type,
removing a family, and a family removal leaving `errors` and `error`
alone when `error/` goes. The behavior is what it was, including one
detail the tests do not pin down because no caller depends on it: the
walk starts after the family name itself, so a mark type that is exactly
`error/` would survive a removal of `error/`.

Between #40 and this one the header is down to the map merge operator,
and that is the last piece.

commits.summary: Replace oak::replace_copy with text::replace_all (#43)
commits.body:
The fourth piece of taking `oak/algorithm.h` apart, after #40, #41 and
#42.

`oak::replace_copy` swapped every occurrence of one substring for
another. The name suggested `std::replace_copy`, which swaps single
elements and is a different thing, and the seven iterator arguments made
each of the three callers a line too long to read.

All three callers work on a `std::string`. The save path converts line
endings, and the two command runners put a command's name where its
temporary script path shows up in output. So the replacement is a plain
string function, `text::replace_all(str, find, replacement)`, in the
text framework beside `text::trim`, and each caller is one line.

It comes with tests. One of them pins down a behavior the old template
did not have: an empty search string leaves the input alone rather than
looping forever. No caller passes an empty search string, so nothing
observable changes.

commits.summary: Move the test shuffle helper into a test-only header (#42)
commits.body:
The third piece of taking `oak/algorithm.h` apart, after #40 and #41.

`oak::random_shuffle` exists because `std::random_shuffle` left the
language in C++17 and `std::shuffle` wants a random number engine handed
to it. Only tests call it, sixteen times across six files, to insert
keys in an order they did not choose.

It moves to `Shared/include/test/shuffle.h` as `test::shuffle`, beside
the `jail.h` and `bundle_index.h` helpers that are already test-only.
Same engine, same seeding, the six test files include it, and
application code no longer sees a shuffle it never used.

commits.summary: Replace oak::contains and oak::has_prefix with the standard library (#41)
commits.body:
The second piece of taking `oak/algorithm.h` apart, after #40.

`oak::contains` and both `oak::has_prefix` overloads predate the
standard library having the same thing. The build compiles as C++23 now,
and the standard covers all of it:

- `std::string::contains` and `std::string::starts_with` where the
haystack is a string
- `std::ranges::contains` where it is an array or a vector, which drops
the `std::begin(x), std::end(x)` pair at each of those callers
- `std::ranges::starts_with` where the caller already holds a pair of
iterators, the encoding sniffers

commits.summary: Drop the DB_VAR macro and the header that existed for it (#39)
commits.body:

C++17 says the same thing as `[[maybe_unused]]`, with no per-build
conditional, and Objective-C++ takes it too. The three uses, in the
property list conversion, the text view's drop handling and the file

showIn:at:image:hidePrevious:]`. There are no tests: the result is a

commits.summary: Find in Project on a folder and something inside it searches the folder, not its parent (#32)
commits.body:
Find in Project on the file browser's selection needs one folder to
stand for the selected items: it becomes the search folder, the base for
the glob options, the base that result paths are shown relative to, and
the reason the Find button is enabled. That folder was found by walking
the paths character by character to the first difference and cutting
back to the last separator passed.

That walk has a hole. For a folder selected together with something
inside it, `/foo/bar` with `/foo/bar/baz`, it reaches the end of the
shorter path without meeting a difference, and the last separator it
passed is the one before `bar`. So it answered `/foo`, and the search
covered the folder's parent.

The folder is taken by path component now: split each path, keep the
leading components they all share, join. A shared name prefix that is
not a shared folder, `/foo/bar` beside `/foo/barn`, still answers
`/foo`, nothing in common still answers the root, one path is still
itself, and a trailing separator changes nothing.

The Find framework had no tests. It has nine now, over this function,
and the first commit on the branch holds the version that recorded the
old answer beside the one that expected the right one, so the failure is
on record before the fix.

commits.summary: Bundle commands run on a pinned Ruby through rv and the Runtimes bundle, never the system Ruby (#29)
commits.body:
Bundle commands run on a Ruby the application pins. A new mandatory
bundle finds or installs it through [rv](https://rv.dev), Spinel's Ruby
manager. The system Ruby is never used.

## The split

The application keeps the small, stable part. It names the pinned
version, 4.0.6, as a constant. At launch it runs the bundle's resolver
off the main thread and remakes the command environment around the
answer. The answer goes first on `PATH` and into `TM_RUBY`. The
application also refuses the system Ruby, and logs what the resolver
reported on the way.

The [Runtimes bundle](https://github.com/textmate3/runtimes.tmbundle)
carries the machinery that should move without an application release.
It holds Spinel's `rv` binary with its licenses, and two shell scripts.
They are shell because they run before any Ruby exists. `ruby_runtime
<version>` finds the version wherever rv looks, or installs it, and
answers on standard output with a one word protocol: `ruby`,
`installed`, `fallback` or `error`. `project_ruby <directory>` answers
with the Ruby a project pins, for the person's own code. That one is
written but not called yet. The bundle has nine tests of its own over a
stand-in rv.

## The rule

A `TM_RUBY` naming `/usr/bin/ruby` or anything under the system's Ruby
framework is refused. The command says so on its standard error and runs
on the application's Ruby instead. The environment keeps that Ruby a
second time as `TM_APPLICATION_RUBY` for this purpose. With no Ruby
known at all, a command with a Ruby shebang is rewritten to decline with
a message rather than fall through `/usr/bin/env` to the system. Any
other absolute `TM_RUBY` wins, as it always has.

Five tests in the command framework cover those cases. Nine in the io
framework cover the resolver's protocol, a run against a stand-in
resolver, and the system Ruby's names.

## What else changed

- rv's `RUBIES_PATH` replaces its search list rather than adding to it.
One directory in it that does not exist makes every lookup fail. The
scripts name only directories that exist, rv's own and chruby's
included.
- The bundle is mandatory in the catalog, so an existing installation
picks it up at the next index refresh. The bundles manager already
installs a mandatory bundle that is missing. The bundle is also seeded
for first launch.
- The other seed archives are left as they were. Five are behind their
bundles, and refreshing them is a change of its own.
- The vendored rv, the earlier rv code and its tests, and the series
lookup from the spike are gone from the application.

The catalog change that makes the bundle mandatory is on a branch of its
own in the catalog repository.

commits.summary: A standalone helper beside the application's executable is signed as itself (#28)
commits.body:
A build rule fix found while vendoring a helper into the application
during the Ruby runtime spike, carried over on its own since it stands
regardless of what that spike decides.

The nested signing rule decides what bundle an executable belongs to
from its path, and it took any binary under `Contents/MacOS` for the
application's own executable. So a helper copied beside the executable
and listed for re-signing was never signed: the rule signed the whole
application in its place, early and before its resources were in, and
the helper kept its vendor's signature. `codesign --verify --deep` was
happy, since the vendor's signature is a valid one, and notarization
would have refused the application for a nested binary under another
team.

Two changes to the rule. A bundle's executable is the one that carries
the bundle's name, `TextMate.app/Contents/MacOS/TextMate` and not
`TextMate.app/Contents/MacOS/rv`, which is the test the framework case
already used. And signing a standalone helper waits for the copy that
puts it in place, since a lone file has nothing under it for the
dependency scan to find.

Nothing in the tree today lists a helper in `MacOS` for nested signing,
so the built application is unchanged by this. The Sparkle pieces keep
going through the same rule as before.

commits.body:

Release builds talk to production regardless of local.rave (#21)
commits.body:
The first two alphas shipped pointing at localhost. The Swift bundle
install from alpha.2 went to a Rails app that happened to be on port
3000, and an update check would have gone there too, so neither alpha
could have updated itself.

The release build loads `local.rave`, because that is where the
Developer ID identity lives, and on the same machine `local.rave` also
points development builds at a catalog and feed on localhost with
development signing keys. Nothing in the release engine looked at what
the application was built to talk to, so every check passed.

Two changes. The per build file the engine writes, now `release.rave`
since it carries more than the prerelease suffix, restates the
production catalog host, bundle key, feed URL and feed key, and is
applied after `local.rave` so it wins. That took a second look: rave
applies the files on a `load` line last to first, so `release.rave` is
named first on the line, and the comment there says why. The values are
read from `default.rave`, where production is defined, not copied. And
after the build, before anything is signed or published, the engine
checks the built application: the feed and key in its Info.plist and the
catalog host and bundle key in its binary must be production, and none
of them may be what `local.rave` overrides them with. Run against the
alpha.2 build, that check refuses it on the feed URL.

The installed alpha.2 cannot receive alpha.3 through Sparkle, since it
asks localhost. Alpha.3 gets installed by hand, and alpha.4 is the
update test.

commits.summary: WIP: Update README toward 2.1 ... 3.0
Two fixes from the first alpha: fetch tags with force, and zip without extended attributes (#20)
commits.body:
Two things the first alpha surfaced in the release engine.

## Tags

The next prerelease number comes from the tags, and the local tags had
gone stale: the `gtm` tag moves with every merge, a plain fetch refuses
to move it and refuses every other tag with it, silently under
`--quiet`, so `v2.1.0-alpha.1` never arrived and a second alpha would
have computed the same number. The engine now fetches tags with force
before numbering, and computes the version after the fetch rather than
at construction.

## The archive

The alpha.1 zip was made with plain `ditto -c -k`, which stores extended
attributes as AppleDouble entries. Unzipped with ditto they fold back
into attributes and every check passes. Unzipped in Finder, Archive
Utility writes them as literal `._` files, 412 of them, and the ones
inside the Sparkle framework are unsealed contents, so the signature
fails and Gatekeeper refuses the application with the "could not verify
it is free of malware" dialog, notarization and staple notwithstanding.
The archive is now made without attributes, resource forks, ACLs or
quarantine, as the notarization submission already was. Deleting the
stray files from the installed copy repaired it, and it opens.

The About window's Legal page listed Onigmo only. It now says what

commits.summary: Markdown lint
A release pipeline with alpha, beta and release channels (#18)
commits.body:
The release pipeline, and the channels it publishes to.

## What changes

- Three release scripts, named so no prefix completes into another:
`script/alpha_release` and `script/beta_release` publish the next
prerelease of their channel with no prompt, and `script/publish_release`
publishes the release to everyone after I type the version back. All
three refuse to run from a branch other than main or with uncommitted
changes. The engine behind them is `script/lib/release.rb`.
- A release notarizes through `script/notarize`, zips the stapled
application, signs the zip with the production Sparkle key from my login
keychain, creates the GitHub Release for the tag with the zip attached
and the commits since the previous tag as notes, and adds the entry to
the appcast in the catalog repository beside this one and pushes, which
is the feed the running application checks.
- Versions are derived, not edited. The version people read is the
notes' newest heading, now `2.1.0`, plus a prerelease suffix such as
`-alpha.3` that the release supplies for one build through an untracked
`prerelease.rave`. The build number, which is what Sparkle compares, is
the commit count offset past the 9800 that earlier builds carried. CI
fetches full history so its count is right.
- Three channels: release, no channel name, everyone; beta, the
nightlies, anyone living on the edge; alpha, the development team. A
prerelease's appcast entry carries its channel. Which entries a copy
sees is the `updateChannel` default: `alpha` sees alphas and betas,
`beta` sees betas, anything else sees releases only.
- `script/prune_releases alpha` removes every alpha from GitHub Releases
and from the feed once betas have taken over, and likewise for betas.
- `Changes.md` gains the `2.1.0` heading with the headline changes,
which is what stamps the build.

## Checked

A plain build reads `2.1.0` with build number 15812. With a prerelease
suffix in place the same build reads `2.1.0-alpha.0`, and `2.1.0` again
once the suffix is removed. The engine computes `2.1.0-alpha.1` as the
next alpha and `2.1.0` as the release, and `script/alpha_release` run
from this branch refuses with "releases come from main". Nothing has
been published: the first alpha is a separate step, since it creates a
public release and changes the live feed.

commits.summary: Notarize on request, and sign Sparkle's Autoupdate helper as itself (#17)
commits.body:
The build notarizes on request. `script/notarize` builds and signs the
release application, zips it, submits it to Apple's notary service under
my `textmate3` keychain profile, waits, fails unless the answer is
Accepted, and staples the ticket. A plain build never notarizes, and the
script refuses to run without a Developer ID identity in `local.rave`.

## Found by the first submission

Apple rejected the first archive for one file, Sparkle's `Autoupdate`,
still carrying its ad hoc signature with no timestamp. The rule that
names the bundle a nested binary belongs to took anything under a
framework's `Versions` directory for the framework's own binary, so
`Autoupdate` was signed as the framework, twice, and never as itself.
The rule now matches the framework only for the binary that carries its
name.

## Checked

The second submission was Accepted, `xcrun stapler validate` passes on
the application, and `spctl -a -t exec` reports it as Notarized
Developer ID. Every embedded piece, `Autoupdate` included, carries the
Team ID and a secure timestamp.

commits.summary: Run the workflow once per push (#16)
commits.body:
Every push to a branch with an open pull request ran the workflow twice,
once for the push event and once for the pull request event, on two
macOS runners. The push trigger now covers main only, so a branch runs
once for its pull request and main runs on each merge. Nothing else in
the workflow changes.

commits.summary: The privileged helper as an SMAppService daemon, retiring the last deprecated call (#15)
commits.body:
The privileged helper becomes a launchd daemon inside the application
bundle, registered with the system through `SMAppService`. That retires
`AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges`, deprecated since macOS 10.7 and
the last deprecated call in the project, along with the pragma that
silenced it. The honest deprecation count is zero emitted and zero
suppressed.

## What changes

-
`Contents/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.textmate3.TextMate.PrivilegedTool.plist`
names the daemon by its path in the bundle,
`Contents/MacOS/PrivilegedTool`, and gives launchd the socket to hold.
`connect_to_auth_server` registers the daemon on first use and, when the
system wants the user's approval, opens Login Items in System Settings
and says so in the log.
- The daemon defines its own authorization right when it starts, since
nothing installs it any more. It quits after two minutes idle, so a
newer build is picked up on the next connection, and steps aside when
the application meets an older one still running.
- The self installer, `install.cc`, and `mate`'s installing of the
helper when run as root are gone. The socket protocol and the read and
write requests stay as they were, with three requests added: make a
directory, copy, remove.
- Installing `mate` into a directory that needs an administrator asks
the daemon for those three instead of running `/bin/mkdir`, `/bin/cp`
and `/bin/rm` as root.
- The helper's names carry the application's identity. TextMate 2's
`com.macromates.auth_server` is left alone, since TextMate 2 still uses
it.

## Checked

The application builds and signs, with the daemon and its job in place
and the daemon carrying the Team ID. The daemon refuses to run

commits.summary: Sign with a Developer ID, and re-sign the vendored Sparkle pieces with the same identity (#14)
commits.body:
The build signs with a Developer ID when one is configured, and signs
everything inside the application with the same identity.

## What changes

- `default.rave` keeps the ad hoc identity, with a comment on where the
real one goes, so anyone can build. A machine with the certificate sets
`CS_IDENTITY` in its untracked `local.rave`.
- The vendored Sparkle framework arrives ad hoc signed. Under the
hardened runtime the application only loads libraries signed by its own
team, so once copied into the application it is re-signed innermost
first: `Installer.xpc`, `Downloader.xpc`, `Autoupdate`, `Updater.app`,
then the framework. The application's build file lists those in
`CS_NESTED`, and `bin/rave` signs each as the bundle it belongs to,
after its files are copied and before the application is signed.
Entitlements are preserved, although Sparkle's pieces carry none.
- The address book entitlement is gone. Nothing reads contacts. Library
validation stays off, and the entitlement's comment says why: an ad hoc
build has no team for Sparkle to match, and third party plug-ins are
signed by whoever wrote them.

## Checked

A release build on the machine with the certificate: `codesign --verify
--deep --strict` passes on the application, the application and every
embedded piece report the Developer ID authority and Team ID, the
application's entitlements are the two that remain, and Gatekeeper
reports "Unnotarized Developer ID", which is what a signed build says
before notarization. Continuous integration builds ad hoc as before,
which exercises the same nested signing with the ad hoc identity.

commits.summary: Give the application its own identity, with a first launch import from TextMate 2 (#13)
commits.body:
The application gets an identity of its own before the first Developer
ID certificate is used, since the certificate, the notarization ticket
and the helper's identifiers all key off it.

## What changes

- The bundle identifier is `com.textmate3.TextMate`. The dialog plug-in
follows as `com.textmate3.plugin.dialog`. `mate` finds the application
by the new identifier.
- The Application Support directory is `~/Library/Application
Support/TextMate 3/`, and the caches folder is
`~/Library/Caches/com.textmate3.TextMate/`. `oak::application_t` is the
one place that knows both, as `support(...)` and the new `cache(...)`,
and the two names are constants beside it. Every place that spelled a
path out, fourteen of them across bundles, the bundle manager,
documents, the pasteboard history, the file browser's favorites, the
encoding menu, plug-ins, `tm_query` and `gtm`, asks it instead. The
encoding framework sits below OakSystem and asks its bundle for the
identifier.
- The first launch on a machine with TextMate 2 imports from it once,
before anything reads either: every preference in
`com.macromates.TextMate` when the new domain is empty, and a copy of
the old Application Support directory when the new one does not exist.
TextMate 2 is left as it was, and after that the two applications no
longer see each other. `FirstLaunchImport.mm` logs what it did under the
new identifier's subsystem.
- Pasteboard types, the command error domain, the JavaScript log
subsystem and the credits and symbolication cache paths carry the new
identifier.

## What stays

The `com.macromates.textmate.*` file type identifiers, which name file
types. The `com.macromates.*` extended attributes documents carry, which
TextMate 2 wrote and the application keeps reading. The `txmt` URL
scheme. The privileged helper's names, which the `SMAppService`
migration replaces.

## Still to do from the decision

Dropping the keys the fork no longer reads waits on an audit of which
defaults keys the application reads, bindings in nibs included. The
import carries every key until then.

## Checked

The application builds with the new identifier in its Info.plist. The
bundles, document, file, FileBrowser, HTMLOutput, io and settings test
binaries pass. The first launch import has not been run: it copies the
real support directory on this machine, so that is a step to take
deliberately.

commits.summary: Edit preferences and macros as forms in the bundle editor (#10)
commits.body:

the set: every property list item kind now has one, and the bundle

commits.summary: Grammar editor: panel edits reach the preview, rule shapes change, capture patterns in the outline (#8)
commits.body:
The gaps the grammar editor's acceptance test left open, in one branch.

captures tables stay, since the form shows the ones the shape uses.
- **Captures with patterns of their own appear in the outline**, under
their rule, labeled by table and number, so their nested patterns can be
selected and edited like any other.
- **The outline uses the inset list style.** The sidebar style is
translucent and showed whatever window sat behind the editor through a

commits.summary: Grammar editor: live preview of sample text parsed with the grammar being edited (#7)
commits.body:
The grammar editor's third increment, and the last part of the plan: the
live preview. Replaces pull request 6, which GitHub closed when the
branch it was stacked on was merged and deleted. Same commits, replayed
onto main, plus the fixes from the hands on test.

## What is here

Under the outline and the form, a third pane in two halves:

- **Sample text**, typed by the person, kept for the session.
- **The same text parsed with the grammar as it is being edited**, by
the parser in `Frameworks/parse`, and colored with the theme a document
would get, dark or light or scoped, painted on the theme's own
background. Selecting in it shows the full scope chain at that point in
a line beneath, the way the Show Scope command does.

It re-renders a quarter of a second after any change to the sample, the
grammar or the appearance, so editing a pattern, renaming a repository
rule, or removing a rule shows its effect on real text at once, next to
the validator's findings.

## How it is wired

`TMGrammarPreviewRenderer`, Objective-C++, takes the sample and the
grammar's dictionary. It wraps the dictionary in a transient bundle item
that is never in the index, builds a `parse::grammar_t` from it, which
resolves includes of other grammars through the bundle index as a real
document would, runs the parser line by line, and builds an attributed
string with the theme's foreground and font per run and the scope as a
custom attribute. The theme is resolved the way the text view resolves
it: a scoped `theme` setting first, otherwise the appearance preference
choosing between the dark mode and universal themes.

Swift reaches it through `BundleEditor-Bridging-Header.h`, the first
bridging header in the tree, which `bin/rave` already knew how to pass.
The header is plain Objective-C, since the Swift compiler cannot read
Objective-C++, and that is the whole reason the renderer's interface is
two methods with Foundation types.

The parser needs the grammar's scope name, which lives in the properties
panel rather than the text pane's four keys, so the bundle editor now
hands the editor the rest of the grammar as context. The context is
read, never written back.

## From the hands on test

- Form values align trailing, as macOS settings forms do, and every
field is a plain single line text field that scrolls within itself when
a pattern runs long. The wrapping field that was there first misaligned
in two ways and swallowed Home and End.
- An empty row in the File Types list, which its plus button adds, used
to be saved as the no string marker and then threw on the next load of
the item, leaving the previous item's title with an empty pane. Upstream
code. Both directions now skip empties.

## Checked by hand

A typed JSON sample came back colored in the current theme in both
appearances. Clicking a word showed its scope chain. Editing the
`constant` rule's pattern uncolored `true` a moment later and colored it
again when put back. Undo, redo and every arrow key combination behave
as in any text field. Saved edits took effect in the editor after a
relaunch.

## Not yet

preview only after the item is reloaded. A sample taken from the
bundle's own test file. Highlighting the text the selected rule matched.
A capture's nested patterns, and changing a rule's shape after it is
made.

commits.summary: Grammar editor: add, remove and move rules, captures and repository names (#5)
commits.body:
The grammar editor's second increment: rules can be added, removed and
moved, captures added and removed, and repository entries renamed. With
this the form covers what the property list text pane could do for a
grammar, short of the preview.

## What is here

- **The bar under the outline.** A plus menu adds a match rule, a begin
and end rule, or an include, either after the selection or nested inside
it, and adds a repository rule. A minus removes the selection. Up and
down move it within its list. Every row's context menu offers the same
for that row.
- **Captures.** Each captures table has a plus in its header that adds
the next number, and each row a minus. The capture's number or name is
editable.

rule's fields, editable, so a `#name` can be renamed. The outline label
follows, and the validator footer reports every include that pointed at
the old name until they are updated.
- **Where things happen.** Adding, removing and moving live on
`GrammarDocument`, one method each, and the views only call them. A rule
is found by its place, the document's own patterns or a rule's, and
removed from wherever it sits: a pattern, a repository entry, an
injection, or a capture's rule, which removes the capture.

parent so the new rule is in view.

appears below it, selected, with empty fields, a capture added to it and
removed, the rule moved down and removed, a nested match rule added into

commits.summary: Grammar editor: rules as an outline and a form, in place of the text pane (#4)
commits.body:
The second step of the structured grammar editor, on top of the schema:
the bundle editor edits a grammar as a form instead of as property list
text. First increment, meant to be looked at before it grows.

## What is here

Selecting a grammar in the bundle editor replaces the text pane with a
two pane editor:

- **Outline**, left. The grammar's patterns with their nesting, then the
repository by name, then the injections by selector. Each row shows the
rule's scope or what it matches or includes, and its shape.
- **Form**, right. The selected rule's fields, chosen by its shape:
match with its captures, begin and end with theirs and a content name,
begin and while, or an include. Labels and hover help come from the
schema's key table. Fields wrap, since patterns run long. An emptied
field removes the key.
- **Issues**, bottom. What `GrammarValidator` finds in the grammar as it
is edited, one line per issue with the path to the rule, or nothing.

Every edit goes straight into the grammar's dictionary. There is no
parse step, so nothing the loader cannot read can be produced, and keys
the schema does not know are carried through untouched. Saving is the
bundle editor's existing path with the same four keys it saved before,
`comment`, `patterns`, `repository` and `injections`. The grammar's
name, scope, file types and first line match stay in the properties
panel beside it. Every other item kind still gets the text pane.

## How it is wired

`Frameworks/BundleEditor` gains Swift: a model tree, `GrammarDocument`
over `GrammarRule`, `GrammarCapture` and `GrammarNamedRule`, loaded from
the dictionary and serialized back; the SwiftUI views; and
`GrammarEditorController`, the Objective-C facing controller with three
methods and a callback. `BundleEditor.mm` puts the controller's view in
the document pane for grammars, asks it whether it is edited, takes its
dictionary in `commitEditing`, and tells it when the item was saved. The
document pane became a container view whose one subview is either the
text view or the editor, because a split view controller keeps the view
it took at insertion.

Two `bin/rave` changes came with it, each its own commit: Swift module
imports and the header waits before a Swift step follow a target's
direct requires only. The tree's transitive requires form loops, which
object linking tolerates and module compilation cannot, and the first
Swift module inside a framework others require found them.

## Checked by hand

On the Ruby bundle's grammar: the outline reads right, selecting a rule
shows the fields for its shape, editing a name marks the window modified
at once, saving writes the change into the local delta bundle, selecting
a command afterwards brings the text pane back. On the Matlab bundle's
MATLAB grammar, the issues footer lists the same findings the sweep
found.

## Not yet

Adding, removing and reordering rules. Editing a capture's nested
patterns beyond its scope. The live preview.

commits.summary: GrammarSchema: the grammar format as data, with a validator (#3)
commits.body:
The first step of the structured grammar editor: the grammar format
written down once as data, so the form, the validator and any sweep
build on the same tables instead of their own lists. Nothing in the
application uses it yet. That is the next branch, the form hosted in the
bundle editor where the text pane is now.

## What is here

`Frameworks/GrammarSchema`, the first Swift only framework, four types
and a validator:

- `GrammarSchema`: the keys a grammar's top level may carry and the keys
a rule may carry, each with the kind of value behind it and a line of
help for the form. The rule keys are exactly the sixteen the parser in
`Frameworks/parse` reads, plus `disabled` and `comment`. Two more tables
say which rule keys exclude each other and which need another present.
- `GrammarValueKind`: text, regular expression, scope name, scope
selector, boolean, text list, captures, patterns, repository,
injections, include. One field per kind, later.
- `GrammarRuleShape`: match, begin and end, begin and while, include, or
patterns only, decided from the keys present.
- `GrammarValidator`: takes the dictionary a `.tmLanguage` loads into
and reports unknown keys, conflicting keys, missing partners, `#name`
includes that resolve nowhere through the enclosing repositories the way
the parser resolves them, and values of the wrong kind. Each issue
carries a path a person can follow,
`repository.blocks.patterns[2].patterns[1]`. It does not compile regular
expressions, which needs the parser's Oniguruma and belongs to whatever
hosts the form.

Tests are Swift Testing over two fixtures: the collection's JSON
grammar, which must validate clean, and a grammar written to trip every
check.

`Applications/validate_grammar`, a command line tool over the validator:
give it grammar files, it prints the issues with their paths and exits
nonzero when there are any, so a bundle's tests can run it.

that holds `textmate/` and `bundles/`:

commits.summary: Swift Testing under script/test (#2)
commits.body:
Swift Testing under `script/test`, the second of the decisions the Swift
spike raised. Nothing about how tests are run changes for anyone:
`script/test` and CI call the same `<target>/test/run` phonies as
before, and those now depend on a Swift runner too when a target has
Swift tests.

## How it works

- A target lists Swift tests the way it lists C++ ones, in `tests`, and
`bin/rave` partitions them by extension. The `.swift` files compile as a
`<Target>Tests` module together with a generated `main.swift` holding
the entry point SwiftPM uses, `Testing.__swiftPMEntryPoint()`, which
discovers every `@Test` and exits nonzero when one fails.
- The module links against the same objects as the C++ test runner, plus
the platform's `Testing.framework` with an rpath to it, and the Testing
macros come from the toolchain's plugin directory. Both paths are asked
of `xcrun` when the build file is generated, the same way the SDK path
is.
- The result is `_Tests/<Target>_swift_test` next to
`_Tests/<Target>_test`. Both hang off `<target>/test` and
`<target>/test/run`.
- `Frameworks/OakFoundation/tests/ApplicationInfoTests.swift` is the
first suite, the same round trip its Objective-C++ neighbor
`t_application_info.mm` checks, so the two runners can be compared on
identical ground.

## What it does not do

- `@testable import`: the modules compile with `-O`, which disables
testability, so Swift tests see a target's public API only, the same as
the Objective-C++ tests do through the generated header. Adding
`-enable-testing` to debug builds is a one line follow-up if a test ever
needs internals.
- Anything for targets without Swift tests. The C++ path is the same
code moved under a guard.

Swift and SwiftUI spike: ApplicationInfo, the About page, and the encoding chooser sheet (#1)
commits.body: The first Swift and SwiftUI in the tree, as a spike: three pieces, each the smallest real thing that answers one question about building Swift inside the application as it is built today. All three work and are meant to stay. ## The three pieces 1. **Swift only.** `ApplicationInfo` in `Frameworks/OakFoundation`: the version and copyright from Info.plist, seen from Objective-C as `OakApplicationInfo`. The About window reads it. An Objective-C++ test constructs it through the generated header. 2. **SwiftUI, not interactive.** The About page of the About window is a SwiftUI view in an `NSHostingView`, swapped in for the web view when that page is selected. The other four pages stay HTML. The page now states the copyright, the absence of warranty, and links the GPL 3 license file, which the old page could not since Info.plist has no copyright string. 3. **SwiftUI, interactive.** The encoding chooser sheet: a model, the view, a preview wrapping the existing NSTextView rendering through `NSViewRepresentable`, and an Objective-C facing controller. `EncodingWindowController` keeps its interface and the document layer did not change. Verified end to end: pick an encoding, the preview follows, Open decodes the file in it, the classifier learns it, the next launch preselects it. ## What the build learned - `bin/rave` compiles a target's Swift sources as one module named after the target, whole module, one object. The step writes the module and the header Objective-C sees the module through, exported like the target's own headers, so dependents write `#import `. A target's Swift can import the Swift modules of the targets it requires. A `Target-Bridging-Header.h` next to the sources is supported and none of the three pieces needed one. - Swift 6 with strict concurrency, set once in `default.rave`. It bit once: a shared static instance of an NSObject subclass needs `@unchecked Sendable`. - The Swift runtime comes from the operating system. Thin LTO and dead stripping on the C++ side are untouched. The application binary grew by 120 KB. - Swift steps cost 0.2 to 2.4 seconds from the ninja log. The slowest C++ step in the tree is 5.3 seconds. - `script/format` and `script/lint` wrap `swift format` and SwiftLint. `.swift-format` asks for tabs, matching the rest of the tree, and 200 columns. - Swift Testing is not wired. The Swift test runs under the existing C++ runner from an Objective-C++ file. A runner for Swift Testing is a decision for later. ## A bug found on the way Since the property list caches landed, the encoding classifier never saved: its words are bytes in the charset being learned, not UTF-8, and a property list key must be a string, so the write failed silently. The words are base64 keys in the file now. ## Decisions this raises - Tabs in `.swift-format`, or swift format's default two spaces. - A runner for Swift Testing, or Swift kept testable from Objective-C++ through the generated header. - Keeping the three pieces as they are, which is the recommendation.

commits.body:
The tool wrote the bundle index cache in seven formats and read each back, ten rounds interleaved, on an Apple M1 with 52 bundles, 2519 bundle items and 2556 cache entries, machine in use, load average around 3. Median load from disk to a populated cache:

  capnp packed          5.9 ms   957778 bytes
  plist binary         15.0 ms   899199 bytes
  json                 14.7 ms   907881 bytes
  jsonl                17.3 ms   912994 bytes
  csv                  17.0 ms   920973 bytes
  yaml                 18.0 ms  1027103 bytes
  plist xml            26.2 ms  1530809 bytes

Every format round tripped without loss. An index build from nothing, every bundle file read and parsed, took 112 ms after the first build in a process, and 384 ms for the first, which pays for paging in the parsing code and warming the regular expression and property list machinery. The application launched hidden, five times of each kind: 406 ms with no cache and 306 ms with a warm one, the cache load being 7 ms and the index build 20 ms of the warm launch.

So the cache is worth about a hundred milliseconds per launch and the format about ten. A plain format is close enough that nobody can feel it, and binary property list was chosen because the cache already knew how to write and read one. CSV and YAML were ruled out by shape rather than speed, since neither holds nested values without another format inside a cell.

Report page errors from HTML output to the application. The legacy view had an undocumented addMessageToConsole: hook, which the migration dropped; this is the supported equivalent, hooking window error events, unhandled promise rejections and console error and warn. It matters more than it did before: a bundle that wraps a bridge call in try/catch and discards the result, which the git gateway does, would otherwise swallow the guidance the bridge throws and fail with no trace anywhere. Git Config saving silently was exactly that

Attach the stream handlers before starting a command. Construction used to spawn the process and begin reading, while the handlers were attached a few lines later, so anything written in that window was buffered and never streamed. A command that writes immediately would lose its first chunk, which for a page that renders only from onreadoutput means losing the beginning of its content. Starting is now a separate call the bridge makes once the handlers are in place

Keep a command's output job registered until its page has been read. A command finishing does not mean the web view has asked for its output: loading is asynchronous, so a fast command completes before the request arrives, and unregistering at completion left nothing to serve. That is what produced a frame load interruption for quick commands like Git Status while a slow one like a Ruby script with a sleep in it worked. The pipe's read end still holds everything written, so the handler now clears the job when it reads to the end instead. This is also the real cause of the failure attributed to unsynchronised registry access earlier; the lock is still correct, but it was not the bug

Reinstate the JavaScript bridge on WKWebView, asynchronously. The page half is a user script injected at document start, registered on the configuration once rather than attached per navigation, since the window-object hook it used before does not exist. The application half answers through a reply handler, because there is no synchronous path from a page into the host process. Most of the old surface is unchanged: passing a callback works, and cancel, write, close and the streaming handlers still reach the running command. Only reading outputString or errorString off the return value cannot work, since both need the command to have finished, and that case throws an error naming the property and showing both replacements rather than yielding undefined and rendering wrong output silently. The fifteen second warning for long synchronous commands goes with the synchronous mode it existed to police

Synchronise the scheme handler's job registry, and report the URL that actually failed. Registration runs on whichever queue the command's output handler is on, while lookup runs on the main thread when the content process asks for the page, and an unsynchronised NSMutableDictionary gives no visibility guarantee across that boundary. The symptom was a job registered and then not found moments later, so the page never loaded and WebKit reported a frame load interruption instead. Every access takes a lock now. The error page also reported (null) as the failing URL, because a provisional failure leaves the web view without one; it comes from the error's user info instead
Remove the protocol relative URL helper, whose only caller went with the resource load delegate

Finish the WebKit migration in the application, leaving the JavaScript bridge. The txmt link interception moves to the navigation delegate, and the delegate methods that no longer have a counterpart are deleted rather than left compiling against protocols nothing implements. Three behaviours go with them and are recorded where they were: the tm-file to file rewrite, protocol relative URL fixing, and the not-found error page, all of which lived in the resource load delegate, for which WKWebView offers no equivalent because subresource requests cannot be rewritten. Link clicks can still be handled in the navigation delegate; subresources cannot. The status bar's link preview on hover goes the same way. No legacy WebKit symbol remains outside the bridge

Move find, selection and view source in HTML output windows off the synchronous DOM. All three reached into the document directly, which is not possible when the content lives in another process. Searching goes through findString:withConfiguration:, whose three options map exactly onto the old ones; selection comes back from window.getSelection through JavaScript; and view source asks the page for its markup, which arrives already decoded and so retires the encoding branches the old code carried. Every caller is a menu action or the find server, none of which needed an answer inline

Replace the NSURLProtocol that served command output with a WKURLSchemeHandler. NSURLProtocol properties do not survive the crossing into the content process, so the output pipe and process identifier move from the request to a registry keyed by URL, which OakCommand populates before loading and clears when the command ends. The properties only the application side reads stay on the request. The handler also serves the page's own assets from disk, which is what makes the styling work: a page from a custom scheme cannot load file:// subresources, but can load them through the same scheme. That deletes 73 lines of NSURLProtocol subclass and the registerURLSchemeAsLocal call with it

Move the HTML output browser view, its delegates and auto-scroll to WKWebView. The frame-based API is gone: loads, stopping, title and history now go to the web view directly, and the request that was loaded is remembered by the view because WKWebView does not expose it. Progress reporting moves from three notifications to key value observing on estimatedProgress. The three panel callbacks gain completion handlers, since the content process cannot be blocked waiting for a modal answer, and window creation moves to the configuration-based delegate method. Auto-scroll is reimplemented inside the page with a MutationObserver, because the document view it used to observe lives in another process now. The JavaScript bridge is not yet installed: didClearWindowObject has no equivalent and user scripts are the replacement, so TextMate.system is unavailable until that lands

Stop the HTML output public interface naming WebView, ahead of replacing it. The header exposed the web view itself, which meant every consumer was coupled to the web engine class even though only three call sites used it, and two of those were one hack: reaching through to the UI delegate to invoke webViewClose:. That is now closeAsIfRequestedByPage, which says what the caller wants rather than how it currently happens, and the focus case is contentView typed as a plain NSView. Nothing outside the HTMLOutput framework names a legacy WebKit class now, apart from registerURLSchemeAsLocal: in OakCommand, which the migration proper replaces
